title: Basement insulation and heat loss
h1: Foundations and basements: keeping heat in below grade
description: Basements can account for about 25% of a home's heat loss. Fix moisture first, seal the rim joist, choose inside or outside insulation and plan for radon.
blurb: Fix water first, seal the rim joist, then insulate, and test for radon before you finish.
lede: NRCan estimates basements can account for about 25% of a home's total heat loss, and many have little or no insulation. The order matters: control water first, seal the rim joist, then insulate, and test for radon before you finish the space.

sections.h2: How heat and moisture escape through a basement
sections.html:
A basement loses heat through a large, often uninsulated surface both above and below grade, and the soil around it is a poor insulator. NRCan's Keeping the Heat In guide puts the basement at about 25% of a home's total heat loss (NRCan ↗). Most of that leaves through the upper part of the foundation wall, which is why basement floor slabs are seldom insulated (NRCan ↗).

Air leaks add to the loss, through basement windows, cracks, service penetrations and the sill plate and rim joist (the header), where the house framing sits on the concrete. NRCan says that band is prone to air leakage and seldom properly insulated (NRCan ↗), and in winter the stack effect draws cold air in through it (NRCan ↗).

Moisture moves in too. Groundwater can wick through concrete and evaporate on the wall, and in humid summer weather, warm air condenses on cool foundation walls (NRCan ↗). CMHC calls moisture “the most common problem in basements” (CMHC ↗).

Crawl spaces and slabs

NRCan treats a heated crawl space as a short basement: insulate its walls rather than the floor above, so pipes and ducts stay warm, and cover the earth floor with a moisture barrier. Slab-on-grade houses are insulated like the outside of a basement wall, with a sloped layer of foam in the ground on frost-susceptible soil (NRCan ↗).

How much insulation is enough?

For retrofits, NRCan recommends basement walls of RSI 3.3 (R-19) where a location has fewer than 3,000 heating degree-days (a measure of how cold the climate is), RSI 4.2 (R-24) from 3,000 to 4,999, and RSI 5.3 (R-30) at 5,000 and above (NRCan ↗). RSI is the metric R-value; multiply by 5.678 to get R. Toronto has about 3,520 degree-days, Ottawa 4,440 and Edmonton 5,120 (National Building Code ↗).

New homes without a heat recovery ventilator must meet minimum effective values, which count the framing, of RSI 1.99 to 3.97 (about R-11 to R-23) on foundation walls, and rim joists must match the above-ground wall requirement (National Building Code ↗).

• Staining or mould, blistering or peeling paint, efflorescence (a white, chalky mineral deposit), crumbling concrete or a musty smell (NRCan ↗).
  • Condensation on foundation walls in summer (NRCan ↗), or on windows and pipes (CMHC ↗).
  • Lifting floor tiles, damp carpet, rust at the base of steel posts, or decaying wood where it touches concrete (CMHC ↗).
  • Drafts, dust or pests getting in along the top of the foundation wall, at the rim joist (NRCan ↗).
  • Cracks that grow or shrink; NRCan advises professional help to check whether structural repairs are needed (NRCan ↗).

NRCan's simple moisture test: tape a 1 m (40 in.) square of plastic to the wall and floor for a day or two. Moisture on top of the plastic points to high indoor humidity. Moisture underneath means water is moving in from the ground, and possibly radon with it (NRCan ↗).

In an EnerGuide evaluation, an NRCan-registered energy advisor records the insulation levels of your walls, ceilings and basement and measures airtightness with a blower door (NRCan ↗). In a basement, the most useful checks are:

  • A blower door test, which depressurizes the house so leaks at the rim joist, windows and penetrations can be traced (NRCan ↗).
  • Thermal imaging under blower door pressure, which NRCan calls “a powerful tool to locate air leaks and missing insulation” (NRCan ↗).
  • Access to crawl spaces and mechanical equipment; NRCan asks homeowners to clear a path to both before the visit (NRCan ↗).
  • The foundation type (poured concrete, block, brick, rubble or stone, or preserved wood), which shapes whether insulation can go inside, outside or both (NRCan ↗).

An energy evaluation is not a home inspection (NRCan ↗). Water, cracks and soil gas may also call for a basement specialist and a long-term radon test.

Inside or outside?

NRCan says outside is best, but inside is often the practical choice. Outside work lets you repair cracks and leaks, keeps the foundation warm and suits rubble, brick and leaky foundations, but it cannot be done in winter, and steps, driveways and landscaping can get in the way. Inside work can be done in stages, often by the homeowner, but only on a dry wall: it makes the concrete colder and can hide moisture problems (NRCan ↗).

• Insulating a damp basement from inside. NRCan says to correct leaks, dampness and efflorescence first “or your new walls will rot” (NRCan ↗). If future flooding seems unavoidable, CMHC advises against interior insulation or finishes that water will damage (CMHC ↗).
  • Plastic against the concrete, or two vapour barriers. Polyethylene on basement walls has caused condensation and mould inside walls. NRCan recommends house wrap behind a framed wall, and no polyethylene over a wall that already has foam board; use a “smart” vapour retarder or the airtight drywall approach instead (NRCan ↗).
  • Stuffing fibreglass into gaps. Glass and mineral fibre do not stop air; NRCan says stuffing them into header gaps “is not effective” (NRCan ↗).
  • Too much foam on cast-in joists. Where joists are embedded in the concrete, NRCan caps foam at 25 mm (1 in.) so the floor above stays warm (NRCan ↗).
  • Heavy interior insulation on stone or rubble. NRCan limits these walls to RSI 2.1 (R-12) inside because of freeze–thaw risk (NRCan ↗).
  • Rushing new concrete. Allow about a year of drying before insulating a new foundation (NRCan ↗).
  • Exposed foam, insulation around flue pipes, a dryer venting into the crawl space, or tar paper indoors. NRCan flags each as a fire, safety or moisture hazard (NRCan ↗).

sections.h2: Radon and soil gas: test before you finish
sections.html:
Radon is a radioactive gas from the ground with no colour, odour or taste. NRCan notes it may be present in any home, and the only way to know is to test (NRCan ↗; NRCan ↗). Health Canada recommends a long-term test of at least 3 months (Health Canada ↗) and a certified radon mitigation professional if the result is above the Canadian guideline of 200 Bq/m³ (Health Canada ↗).

The most common fix uses a pipe and small fan to draw soil gas from under the floor to the outdoors, and mitigation cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Sealing entry routes alone has limited effect (Health Canada ↗).

New homes built to the 2020 code need an air barrier against the ground and a rough-in for a future radon system (National Building Code ↗). In an older basement, NRCan notes insulation can be tied in with waterproofing, radon remediation or finishing, so plan them together (NRCan ↗).

Programs open and close often, so check our rebates by province for what is available now. In Ontario, start with Home Renovation Savings assessments. Some programs include a post-upgrade EnerGuide evaluation that needs proof of the work, so keep paid invoices and receipts (NRCan ↗).

To compare this work with other upgrades at your local fuel prices, try the upgrade payback calculator, then put the order of work into your home plan. You can also find a registered energy advisor near you.

faq.q: How much heat does a basement lose?
faq.a: NRCan estimates a basement can account for about 25% of a home's total heat loss, mostly through the upper part of the foundation walls and through air leaks at the rim joist and basement windows.

faq.q: Is it better to insulate basement walls from the inside or the outside?
faq.a: NRCan says outside is best, especially for rubble, brick or leaky foundations, but inside is often more practical and affordable. Only insulate inside once the wall is dry.

faq.q: Do basement walls need a vapour barrier?
faq.a: It depends on the assembly. NRCan now recommends house wrap rather than polyethylene against the concrete, and warns that polyethylene over foam board creates a double vapour barrier; a smart vapour retarder or sealed drywall is used instead. Check local code.

faq.q: Should I insulate my rim joists?
faq.a: Yes, after sealing them. NRCan calls the rim joist area prone to air leakage and seldom properly insulated, and the 2020 building code requires rim joists in new homes to match the above-ground wall insulation.

faq.q: Should I test for radon before finishing my basement?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test of at least 3 months, and mitigation by a certified professional if levels are above 200 Bq/m³. Testing first lets you plan any radon system before the walls are finished.

faq.q: Do I need to insulate the basement floor?
faq.a: Usually not for energy alone, since most heat leaves through the upper walls. NRCan suggests a moisture barrier or sealed floor for comfort, moisture control and radon reduction, and insulation if you are replacing the slab.

title: Wall insulation for older homes
h1: Walls: finding and filling the gaps in older houses
description: Walls can account for about 20% of a home's heat loss. How balloon framing, empty cavities, dense-pack fill, re-siding and solid masonry change the fix.
blurb: Older frame walls are often partly empty, and many can be filled without opening them up.
lede: NRCan estimates walls can account for about 20% of a home's heat loss, before counting the air that leaks through cracks and penetrations. Older frame walls may be partly or completely empty, and many can be filled without opening them up.

sections.html:
Heat moves through a wall by conduction through solid materials, by convection as air circulates in open spaces, and by radiation. In an uninsulated cavity, air picks up heat on the warm side and gives it up on the cold side (NRCan ↗). Insulation stops that by trapping still air, but only if it fills the space completely and evenly (NRCan ↗).

Framing leaks heat too. A stud is a thermal bridge, a solid path from the warm side to the cold side. NRCan's example: R-20 (RSI 3.52) batts in a 2×6 wall perform like R-17 (RSI 2.99) once the studs and plates are counted, and foam board over the framing acts as a roadblock to that heat flow (NRCan ↗).

Know your wall

  • Frame walls have a cavity to fill. In older houses it is often only 89 to 102 mm (3½ to 4 in.) deep, which limits how much can be added (NRCan ↗).
  • Balloon framing was common up to the early part of the 20th century. Its studs run past the floors to the roof framing, so wall cavities connect floor to floor unless fire blocks were added (CMHC ↗). CMHC lists balloon-frame walls among the hidden air paths into the attic (CMHC ↗), and NRCan notes these open cavities can be the easiest to fill from the attic or basement (NRCan ↗).
  • Brick veneer has a 25 to 50 mm (1 to 2 in.) air space behind the brick for drainage. Do not fill it (NRCan ↗).
  • Solid walls of brick, stone, concrete block, log or plank have no cavity, so insulation must go inside or outside. Many double-brick walls have a gap under 25 mm that drains water; never insulate it or plug its drain holes (NRCan ↗).
  • Concrete block cores can be filled, but the webs and mortar keep conducting heat, so sealing air paths and capping the top course matter more (NRCan ↗).

How much is enough?

For retrofits, NRCan recommends walls of RSI 3.9 (R-22) where a location has fewer than 3,000 heating degree-days, RSI 4.8 (R-27) from 3,000 to 4,999, and RSI 7.1 (R-40) at 5,000 and above (NRCan ↗). Heating degree-days measure how cold a climate is: Toronto has about 3,520 and Winnipeg 5,670 (National Building Code ↗). New homes without a heat recovery ventilator need effective wall values of RSI 2.78 to 3.85 (about R-16 to R-22) (National Building Code ↗).

• Drafts at outlets and switches on exterior walls, and even on interior walls, since air can travel through partitions and along floor joists (NRCan ↗).
  • Staining or mould on exterior walls and ceilings, often in closets and bathrooms (NRCan ↗).
  • Staining, rot, cracked interior or exterior finishes, or windows and doors that stick because they are out of square. NRCan says to fix these moisture or structural problems before insulating (NRCan ↗).
  • Little or nothing in the cavity. NRCan suggests looking behind an outlet on an exterior wall, with the power off, to see what is in the wall (NRCan ↗).

An EnerGuide evaluation records the insulation levels of walls, ceilings and basement and measures airtightness (NRCan ↗). For walls, the most useful checks, by an advisor or an insulation contractor, are:

  • Thermal imaging with the house under blower door pressure, which NRCan calls “a powerful tool to locate air leaks and missing insulation” (NRCan ↗).
  • What is already in the cavities, and what blocks them: fire stops, bracing, wiring, plumbing, windows and doors (NRCan ↗).
  • The wall type (frame, balloon, veneer or solid), which decides whether drill-and-fill is possible at all (NRCan ↗).

An advisor is not a home inspector (NRCan ↗). If the house still has knob-and-tube wiring, have an electrician assess it before any insulation goes in: NRCan warns that insulation must never contact old knob-and-tube wiring because of the fire hazard (NRCan ↗).

Dense-packing suits empty or partly filled frame cavities. Because older stud spaces are shallow, the gains are limited, but NRCan says good results can still be had (NRCan ↗).

• Filling the wrong space. The air gap behind brick veneer and the narrow drainage gap in double-brick walls must stay open, along with their weep holes (NRCan ↗).
  • Blowing insulation over knob-and-tube wiring, a fire hazard (NRCan ↗).
  • Wrong density. Too little leaves voids and settling gaps; too much can make walls bulge. Agree with the installer on the manufacturer's density and the number of bags (NRCan ↗).
  • Leaving holes open. Have exterior holes patched section by section so a storm cannot soak the wall (NRCan ↗).
  • Counting on insulated siding. It adds only RSI 0.35 to 0.70 (R-2 to R-4) and still needs a drainage plane (NRCan ↗).
  • Putting the vapour barrier in the wrong place. At least two-thirds of the wall's insulating value should sit on the cold side of the vapour barrier (NRCan ↗).
  • Believing miracle claims. NRCan says long-term claims above RSI 1.14 per 25 mm (R-6.5 per inch) may not be substantiated, and reflective bubble foils range from RSI 0 to 0.62 (R-0 to R-3.5) (NRCan ↗).
  • Retrofitting solid masonry without advice. NRCan suggests consulting an architect, building conservator or engineer for older and heritage houses (NRCan ↗), and flags freeze–thaw risk when old stone and rubble foundation walls are heavily insulated from inside (NRCan ↗). We found no official Canadian guidance that sets a safe limit for insulating above-grade solid masonry from inside, so get that advice before you start.

NRCan notes walls can be insulated as part of a major repair or renovation, and that exterior insulation can be combined with re-siding (NRCan ↗).

Programs open and close often, so check our rebates by province for what is available now. In Ontario, start with Home Renovation Savings assessments. Some programs include a post-upgrade EnerGuide evaluation that needs proof of the work, so keep paid invoices and receipts (NRCan ↗).

To compare this work with other upgrades at your local fuel prices, try the upgrade payback calculator, then put the order of work into your home plan. You can also find a registered energy advisor near you.

faq.q: Can I insulate existing walls without removing drywall or plaster?
faq.a: Often, yes. Contractors can blow dense-pack cellulose, glass fibre or approved foam into frame cavities through small holes drilled from inside (15 to 50 mm across) or through the siding, then plug and patch them.

faq.q: How do I know if my walls are insulated?
faq.a: With the power off, look behind an outlet cover on an exterior wall, as NRCan suggests. A thermal imaging scan during a blower door test can map missing insulation across the whole house.

faq.q: Is blown-in wall insulation worth it?
faq.a: In empty cavities it adds insulation and improves air sealing. Gains are limited by cavity depth, often only 89 to 102 mm in older houses, but NRCan says good results can still be had.

faq.q: What is balloon framing?
faq.a: A framing method common up to the early 20th century, in which studs run continuously past the floors to the roof framing. Without fire blocks, the wall cavities connect floor to floor and to the attic, which matters for air sealing and fire safety.

faq.q: Should I insulate a brick house from the inside?
faq.a: Solid masonry walls have no cavity, so insulation goes inside or outside. Never fill the narrow drainage gap in double-brick walls, and get advice from an architect, building conservator or engineer before retrofitting an older masonry house.

faq.q: Does insulated vinyl siding help much?
faq.a: Not much. NRCan puts insulated siding at about R-2 to R-4, and suggests R-15 to R-20 of separate exterior insulation when you re-side.

title: Attic insulation, air sealing and ice dams
h1: Roofs and attics: seal first, then insulate
description: How much attic insulation Canadian homes need by climate zone, why air sealing comes first, and how to stop ice dams without adding more vents.
blurb: Stop warm, moist air leaking up from the house first: it drives frost, mould and ice dams.
lede: The attic is a favourite starting point for many homeowners, yet NRCan notes basements and uninsulated walls often lose more heat than a typical attic. The attic's bigger problem is usually warm, moist air leaking up from the house, which drives frost, mould and ice dams.

stats.label: Average ceiling insulation (RSI 5.84) in new homes built 1990–96, from an NRCan field study of 163 houses
NRCan's recommended attic insulation for retrofits, by climate zone (RSI 7.9–14.1)

sections.h2: How heat and moisture escape through the attic
sections.html:
In winter a heated house behaves like a chimney, pushing warm air up through the top-floor ceiling into the attic (CMHC ↗). Leaks around chimneys, vents, plumbing pipes and electrical boxes can account for substantial heat loss, and the moist air they carry condenses or frosts on cold roof sheathing (NRCan ↗). Adding insulation makes the attic colder, so moist air escaping into it is more likely to condense before it can be vented; NRCan calls air sealing the attic “essential” (NRCan ↗).

Insulation then and now

New houses built from 1990 to 1996 averaged RSI 5.84 (R-33) of ceiling insulation in an NRCan field study of 163 homes (NRCan researchers ↗). The code minimum for new homes is now higher, and NRCan recommends more again for retrofits. Heating degree-days measure how cold a climate is:

sections.h2: Signs of trouble in the attic
sections.html:
• Ice dams and icicles at the eaves, or ceiling leaks only in spring, when ice that built up on the sheathing melts (CMHC ↗).
  • Frost on the underside of the roof after a cold snap. Some is normal, but NRCan says buildup of 10 mm (⅜ in.) or more is a reason to check for air leaks and blocked vents (NRCan ↗).
  • Discoloured, dirty-looking patches in the insulation, where it has been filtering air leaking up from below (NRCan ↗; CMHC ↗).
  • Snow melting first over certain spots, such as the hatch, a roof-ducted fan or a plumbing vent, or a horizontal melt line on a 1½-storey house where the knee wall meets the ceiling (NRCan ↗).
  • Water stains or mould on sheathing and rafters, or a mouldy smell in the house, usually in summer (CMHC ↗).
  • Thin insulation at the edges above the outside walls, which leaves cold spots where wall meets ceiling (NRCan ↗).

Clear access to the attic is a condition of an EnerGuide evaluation; the advisor measures ceiling insulation and photographs the attic space (NRCan ↗). An attic inspection looks at:

  • Insulation type, condition, depth and coverage, compared with recommended levels (NRCan ↗).
  • Moisture: roof leaks, stains, mould, rot, frost, and vents blocked by insulation (NRCan ↗).
  • Hazards to deal with before any work: chimney clearances, recessed lights, wiring, animal droppings and vermiculite (NRCan ↗).
  • Air leaks, found with a blower door, which CMHC notes can “amplify the leakage,” and a thermal camera (CMHC ↗; NRCan ↗).

Ice dams form when attic heat melts snow on the roof; the water runs down to the cold overhang, refreezes and backs up under the shingles. Uninsulated attics rarely get them, and neither do well-sealed, well-insulated ones; roofs with many valleys and dormers are more prone (NRCan ↗). The lasting fix is to keep house heat out of the attic by sealing and insulating (NRCan ↗; CMHC ↗). Where a baffle leaves only about 100 mm (4 in.) for insulation at the eaves, spray foam or cut extruded polystyrene helps (NRCan ↗).

Quick fixes fall short. Self-sealing membranes under the shingles, required on the lower roof of new houses, stop leaks but not the ice; heating cables use a significant amount of electricity; chopping at ice damages the roof (NRCan ↗).

Ventilation is the second line of defence. The National Building Code requires vent area of at least 1/300 of the insulated ceiling area, or 1/150 on roofs sloped less than 1 in 6, with at least 25% of the openings high and 25% low (National Building Code ↗). CMHC calls attic ventilation “overrated” and warns that adding vents to a wet attic can pull more moist house air up and make it worse (CMHC ↗).

Cathedral ceilings and flat roofs

Roofs without an attic have little room for insulation or ventilation, and NRCan says they need a qualified contractor (NRCan ↗). Dense-packing eliminates the roof's ventilation, so NRCan says it is generally not recommended without first checking with your building authority; ice dams on these roofs are often best fixed when re-roofing (NRCan ↗; CMHC ↗).

• Adding vents or fans instead of sealing. Electric attic fans can pull house air into the attic, increasing heat loss and moisture (NRCan ↗).
  • Insulation against chimneys. Keep a 75 mm (3 in.) clearance with a non-combustible barrier that rises above the insulation (NRCan ↗).
  • Burying standard pot lights or blocking soffit vents (NRCan ↗).
  • Covering wet insulation. Fix the source and let it dry first (NRCan ↗).
  • Expecting insulation to stop air. NRCan says not to rely on batt, blown or poured insulation in place of air sealing (NRCan ↗).
  • Disturbing vermiculite or droppings. Vermiculite insulation from before 1990 may contain asbestos; leave it alone and read our vermiculite insulation guide before any attic work (NRCan ↗). Bat and bird droppings can grow moulds that cause illness (CMHC ↗).

Programs open and close often, so check our rebates by province for what is available now. In Ontario, start with Home Renovation Savings assessments. Some programs include a post-upgrade EnerGuide evaluation that needs proof of the work, so keep paid invoices and receipts (NRCan ↗).

To compare this work with other upgrades at your local fuel prices, try the upgrade payback calculator, then put the order of work into your home plan. You can also find a registered energy advisor near you.

faq.q: How much attic insulation do I need in Canada?
faq.a: NRCan recommends RSI 7.9 (R-45) in the mildest zone, rising to RSI 14.1 (R-80) where there are 5,000 or more heating degree-days. New homes must meet at least RSI 6.91 to 10.43 effective (about R-39 to R-59).

faq.q: Should I air seal before adding attic insulation?
faq.a: Yes. NRCan calls attic air sealing essential, because more insulation makes the attic colder and leaking house air more likely to condense. CMHC notes a thorough job means clearing insulation from each joist bay to reach the leaks.

faq.q: What causes ice dams?
faq.a: Heat from the house warms the roof and melts snow, which refreezes at the cold eaves. NRCan and CMHC both name air sealing and insulating the attic as the preferred fix.

faq.q: Does my attic need more vents?
faq.a: Usually not. The building code requires vent area of at least 1/300 of the ceiling area, but CMHC calls attic ventilation overrated and says stopping air leaks is the way to fix a wet attic.

faq.q: Is vermiculite attic insulation dangerous?
faq.a: Vermiculite sold before 1990 may contain asbestos. NRCan says it poses very little risk if left undisturbed, so do not move it, and have it assessed before any attic work.

faq.q: Can I insulate a cathedral ceiling?
faq.a: Yes, but it is a job for a qualified contractor. Options include dense-pack insulation, rigid board added under the ceiling, or insulation added from above when the roof is replaced.

title: Windows and doors: when upgrades pay
h1: Windows and doors: what your windows' age tells you
description: U-factors for single, storm, double and triple glazing, ENERGY STAR Canada criteria, and when new windows pay versus sealing or adding storm windows.
blurb: What U-factors say about your windows, and when sealing or storms beat replacement.
lede: Windows, doors and skylights can account for up to 35% of a home's heat loss, according to NRCan. What you gain from upgrading depends on what you have now: a single pane loses about four times as much heat as an ENERGY STAR window, while a sound double-glazed unit may need only sealing.

sections.h2: How heat escapes through windows and doors
sections.html:
Glass conducts heat, cold panes draw radiant heat from your body, and air leaks around sashes and frames (NRCan ↗; NRCan ↗). Radiation is less than 10% of heat loss in most houses, and most of it goes through windows (NRCan ↗). Single-glazed windows lose about 10 to 20 times as much heat as the same area of insulated wall (NRCan ↗). Some “drafts” near windows are cold air sliding down the glass, a convection current rather than a leak (NRCan ↗).

A window's U-factor measures how fast heat passes through the whole unit: glass, edges and frame. Lower is better; it is the inverse of an R-value (NRCan ↗).

Doors

Doors usually matter less than windows simply because there are fewer of them, unless you have patio or garden doors (NRCan ↗). Insulated-core doors resist heat flow better than solid doors or doors with glass (NRCan ↗). Worn weatherstripping, misplaced strike plates, poorly fitting frames and warped doors are the main causes of door air leaks (NRCan ↗).

sections.h2: Signs your windows and doors are costing you
sections.html:
• Fog or condensation between the panes of a sealed unit: the seal has failed, and NRCan says replacing the glazing unit is the lasting fix (NRCan ↗).
  • Condensation between a storm window and the inner window: house air is leaking past the inner sash, which is common upstairs where the stack effect pushes air out (NRCan ↗).
  • Heavy condensation or frost on the room side, usually a sign that humidity is too high for the glass. With the house at 21°C and −20°C outside, NRCan's table shows condensation starting above about 34% indoor humidity on double glazing, 50% on double low-e and 67% on triple low-e (NRCan ↗).
  • Rot, mould or staining around frames, cracked putty or paint, worn weatherstripping, or hardware that no longer closes tightly (NRCan ↗).
  • Doors out of square with their frames, letting drafts in at the edges or threshold (NRCan ↗).

An EnerGuide evaluation records the number, type and location of all windows and exterior doors and measures airtightness with a blower door (NRCan ↗). With the house under pressure, smoke or a thermal camera can show where air leaks in at frames and sashes (NRCan ↗). If condensation is your complaint, ask about humidity and ventilation too; NRCan's suggested solutions start with lowering humidity and improving ventilation (NRCan ↗).

Before working on old windows, doors or trim, consider a lead paint test: homes built before 1950 were often painted with lead-based paint (NRCan ↗).

sections.h2: When replacement pays, and when it doesn't
sections.html:
The U-factors tell most of the story. By our arithmetic from those figures, swapping a single-glazed window (about 5.0) for an ENERGY STAR unit (1.22 or lower) cuts heat flow through that opening by about three-quarters, and replacing a clear double-glazed unit (about 2.9) cuts it by a little over half (PNNL, US DOE ↗; NRCan ↗). Adding a storm panel to a single-glazed window lowers its U-factor by 47 to 53% with clear glass and 59 to 64% with low-e glass (PNNL, US DOE ↗).

Replacement makes the most sense when glazing is single or a sealed unit has failed, or when frames are rotten. NRCan suggests a new sealed glazing insert where the frame is sound and full replacement where it is not; a full tear-out also lets the installer make an airtight, insulated seal to the wall opening (NRCan ↗). It pays least when windows are already double-glazed and sound: NRCan notes some windows need only minor air sealing, and ranks air leakage control first in any upgrade strategy (NRCan ↗; NRCan ↗). Test the numbers for your fuel and climate in the upgrade payback calculator.

The ENERGY STAR Canada criteria

Since January 1, 2020, ENERGY STAR windows and doors sold in Canada must have a U-factor of 1.22 W/m²·K or lower, or an Energy Rating (ER) of 34 or higher, plus air leakage of 1.5 L/s/m² or less; skylights must be 2.29 or lower (NRCan ↗). Products designated Most Efficient for 2025 reach 1.05 or lower, or an ER of 40 or more (NRCan ↗).

Glass also lets in free solar heat, measured as the solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC). For new or substantially renovated homes NRCan suggests an SHGC of 0.3 to 0.4; above 0.4 suits homes built before 1980 or not well insulated and air sealed (NRCan ↗).

• Expecting new windows to cure condensation. Tighter windows can raise humidity and make it worse; reduce moisture and improve ventilation as well (NRCan ↗).
  • Caulking outside first. It can trap warm, moist air in the wall; seal inside, then outside (NRCan ↗).
  • Sealing the storm tighter than the window. With exterior storms the inner window must be the tighter one, and the storm's weep holes must stay open (NRCan ↗).
  • Comparing centre-of-glass ratings. They make a product look more efficient than it is; compare whole-window U-factor or ER (NRCan ↗).
  • Sealing shut or shrinking a bedroom window. Each bedroom needs a window or door that opens from inside, with an opening of at least 0.35 m² and no dimension under 380 mm (National Building Code ↗).
  • Losing the labels. Keep ENERGY STAR labels until any rebate claim is processed (NRCan ↗).
  • Solar-control film on every window. It adds little insulation and cuts useful winter sun (NRCan ↗).

Programs open and close often, so check our rebates by province for what is available now. In Ontario, start with Home Renovation Savings assessments. Some programs include a post-upgrade EnerGuide evaluation that needs proof of the work, so keep paid invoices and receipts (NRCan ↗).

To compare this work with other upgrades at your local fuel prices, try the upgrade payback calculator, then put the order of work into your home plan. You can also find a registered energy advisor near you.

faq.q: Is it worth replacing windows to save energy?
faq.a: It depends on what you have. By our arithmetic from published U-factors, replacing single glazing with ENERGY STAR windows cuts heat flow through those openings by about three-quarters. Replacing sound double-glazed windows saves less, and NRCan puts air sealing first.

faq.q: What U-factor should new windows have in Canada?
faq.a: ENERGY STAR Canada requires 1.22 W/m²·K or lower, or an Energy Rating of 34 or more. Most Efficient 2025 products reach 1.05 or lower, and the 2020 building code caps new windows at 1.44 to 1.84 depending on climate zone.

faq.q: Are storm windows worth it?
faq.a: For sound single-glazed windows they can be. A US national laboratory study found clear storm panels cut single-pane U-factors by 47 to 53%, and low-e storm panels by 59 to 64%.

faq.q: Double or triple glazing for a Canadian winter?
faq.a: Better double-glazed units reach U-factors of 1.2 or lower, and triple-glazed units as low as 0.8. NRCan says triple glazing also helps where glass edges fog up and freeze in more extreme climates.

faq.q: Why do my new windows have condensation?
faq.a: New windows make a house tighter, which can raise humidity. At −20°C outside, NRCan's table shows condensation starting above about 50% indoor humidity on double low-e glass, so lowering humidity or adding ventilation is the usual fix.

faq.q: Should I replace my front door?
faq.a: Weatherstrip and adjust it first, since worn weatherstripping, misplaced strike plates and warped doors are the main causes of leaks. NRCan suggests replacing a badly deteriorated door with an insulated unit.

title: Air sealing and blower door numbers
h1: Air sealing: find the leaks, then seal top and bottom first
description: Air leakage can cause about 25% of a home's heat loss. Blower door results by house age, where leaks hide, what to seal first and how to stay safe.
blurb: Find the leaks with a blower door, seal top and bottom first, and keep combustion safe.
lede: NRCan calls air leakage control the single most important retrofit activity and says it should be considered first. It also changes how the rest of the house behaves, so ventilation and combustion safety are part of the job.

stats.label: of a typical home's heat loss can be due to air leakage
Average leakage of pre-1921 houses in NRCan field data published in 2000; homes built 1991–96 averaged 3.1
more moisture carried by one small air leak than by diffusion through the same area

sections.html:
Air moves through a house wherever there is a hole and a pressure difference. In winter the stack effect does most of the work: warm air rises and pushes out through the ceiling and upper walls, while cold air is drawn in low, through basement windows and the rim joist. The effect grows with leakier houses, taller houses and colder weather, and wind and exhaust appliances add to it (NRCan ↗).

NRCan estimates about 25% of heat loss can be due to air leakage (NRCan ↗). Leaks carry moisture as well: one small air leak can let in 100 times more moisture than diffusion through the same area, and that moisture can condense or frost inside walls and attics (NRCan ↗). The same air movement is why many older houses are very dry in winter (NRCan ↗).

Where the leaks are

  • Top: the attic hatch, plumbing stacks, wiring and light fixtures, chimneys, wall top plates, dropped ceilings, knee walls and balloon-frame walls open to the attic (NRCan ↗; NRCan ↗; CMHC ↗).
  • Bottom: the sill plate and rim joist, service penetrations, basement windows, foundation cracks, floor drains and the base of the chimney (NRCan ↗).
  • In between: outlets and switches (even on interior walls), trim and baseboards, window and door frames, fireplace dampers, exhaust fans, behind tubs and above pocket doors (NRCan ↗).

• Drafts at outlets, baseboards, trim and doors. On a cold, windy day, incense smoke shows where air is moving (NRCan ↗).
  • Very dry indoor air in winter (NRCan ↗).
  • Frost in the attic, ice dams, or discoloured patches in attic insulation where air has been filtering through (NRCan ↗; CMHC ↗).
  • Condensation between storm and inner windows upstairs, where the stack effect pushes air out (NRCan ↗).
  • After sealing: condensation on windows, stale air or lingering odours mean the house now needs more ventilation (NRCan ↗).

Every EnerGuide evaluation includes a blower door test (NRCan ↗). The fan depressurizes the house to 50 pascals, and the result in air changes per hour at that pressure (ACH50) shows how leaky it is; lower is tighter (NRCan researchers ↗; National Building Code ↗). Before the test, fuel-fired heating is turned down or off and the water heater turned down so neither fires while the fan runs, and ashes are cleared from wood-burning appliances (NRCan ↗). Smoke pencils and an infrared camera then pinpoint leaks and missing insulation (NRCan ↗); see thermal imaging.

Regional results varied widely, from 23.6 for pre-1921 houses in BC to 9.1 in the Prairies, and many houses have been sealed since (NRCan researchers ↗). Today the R-2000 standard allows no more than 1.5 ACH50 (NRCan ↗). For energy modelling, the 2020 National Building Code assumes 3.2 ACH50 for a new house built to its basic rules, or 2.5 where the air barrier meets its detailed requirements, and its tiered energy path gives credit for tested levels from 2.5 down to 0.6 (National Building Code ↗).

sections.h2: Fixes, and the order to do them
sections.html:
1. Find the leaks: a blower door, or a DIY fan test with every exhaust fan running. Turn off fuel-fired space and water heaters first (NRCan ↗).
  2. Seal the top and bottom of the house first: the attic floor and hatch, then the rim joist and basement penetrations. This order is our reading of NRCan's guidance rather than a rule it sets: the stack effect pushes air out at the top of the house and draws it in at the bottom (NRCan ↗; NRCan ↗).
  3. Then the middle: outlets, trim, windows and doors. Caulk windows inside before outside (NRCan ↗).
  4. Check ventilation and combustion air before calling the job done (NRCan ↗).

sections.h2: Air sealing and ventilation go together
sections.html:
Tightening a house raises humidity and leaves less air for fuel-burning appliances, so ventilation and combustion air are part of comprehensive air sealing (NRCan ↗). Most older houses still leak enough after sealing to get some fresh air (NRCan ↗), but NRCan says air leakage “does not make for good ventilation” and suggests a system able to change all the house air once every three hours (NRCan ↗). A heat recovery ventilator (HRV) typically recovers 70 to 80% of the heat from the outgoing air, according to Keeping the Heat In (NRCan ↗); NRCan's 2018 ventilation guide gives a wider range of 60 to 90% (NRCan ↗). Aim for indoor humidity of 30 to 50% (NRCan ↗).

Safety: backdrafting and carbon monoxide

When fans, dryers and fireplaces exhaust more air than leaks can replace, the house is depressurized, and a natural-draft furnace, water heater or fireplace can backdraft, spilling combustion gases, including carbon monoxide, into the house (NRCan ↗). Warning signs include soot around appliances, hot and muggy air near the furnace, combustion odours, melted plastic fittings on top of a water heater, and repeated headaches or flu-like symptoms (NRCan ↗).

  • Install CO alarms. In homes with a fuel-burning appliance, code requires one inside each bedroom or within 5 m of each bedroom door (National Building Code ↗).
  • Try NRCan's chimney flow test: with the appliance running, hold incense at the draft hood, then turn on every exhaust fan. If the smoke moves into the room, call a heating contractor (NRCan ↗).
  • Ask for a combustion safety test with any air sealing job; many air sealing companies test for backdrafting (NRCan ↗).

• Stuffing fibreglass into gaps. Glass and mineral fibre are poor air sealing products (NRCan ↗).
  • Ordinary caulk near heat. Chimneys, flues and fan motors need non-combustible sealants (NRCan ↗).
  • Running a fan test with gas or oil heaters on, which risks backdrafting them (NRCan ↗).
  • Exhaust-only ventilation in a tight house. Powerful exhaust fans can depressurize it enough to reverse chimney flow (NRCan ↗).
  • Running several big exhausts at once, such as a high-capacity range hood and a clothes dryer (NRCan ↗).
  • Caulking a bedroom window shut. Building codes require every bedroom to have at least one window that opens from inside (NRCan ↗).

Programs open and close often, so check our rebates by province for what is available now. In Ontario, start with Home Renovation Savings assessments. Some programs include a post-upgrade EnerGuide evaluation that needs proof of the work, so keep paid invoices and receipts (NRCan ↗).

To compare this work with other upgrades at your local fuel prices, try the upgrade payback calculator, then put the order of work into your home plan. You can also find a registered energy advisor near you.

faq.q: What is a good blower door test result?
faq.a: Lower is tighter. In NRCan field data, houses built before 1921 averaged 13.7 ACH50 and homes built 1991 to 1996 averaged 3.1; the 2020 building code uses 2.5 to 3.2 when modelling new homes, and R-2000 homes must test at 1.5 or less.

faq.q: Can a house be too airtight?
faq.a: Not if it is ventilated. Tightening raises humidity and reduces combustion air, so NRCan pairs air sealing with controlled ventilation and checks on fuel-burning appliances.

faq.q: Should I air seal or insulate first?
faq.a: Seal first. NRCan says air leakage control should be considered first in any upgrade strategy, and insulation alone does not stop air.

faq.q: Where do air leaks hide in a house?
faq.a: NRCan's checklist puts many at the top and bottom of the house, where the stack effect pushes air out and pulls it in: attic penetrations, the hatch and wall top plates, and the rim joist and basement openings. Outlets, trim, windows and doors add more.

faq.q: Is it safe to air seal a house with a gas furnace or water heater?
faq.a: Yes, with checks. Install CO alarms, confirm the appliances vent properly with a combustion safety test or chimney flow test, and avoid running several large exhaust fans at once.

faq.q: Can I air seal my house myself?
faq.a: Much of it, yes. NRCan says homeowners can do a relatively effective job with time and patience, though professionals with a blower door usually do better at finding hidden leaks.

title: Indoor humidity and condensation control
h1: Airflow and moisture control: keeping indoor humidity in the safe range
description: Where indoor moisture comes from, the winter humidity levels NRCan, CMHC and Health Canada recommend, and how to stop window condensation and mould.
blurb: Where indoor moisture comes from, the humidity to aim for, and how to stop condensation.
lede: A family of four adds about 50 litres of water a week to indoor air through breathing, cooking, bathing and washing, according to Natural Resources Canada. Whether that moisture leaves through fans or ends up on windows and inside walls decides whether a house stays dry.

stats.label: Moisture a family of four adds to indoor air
Indoor relative humidity range Health Canada recommends
Moisture one small air leak lets in, compared with diffusion over the same area

sections.html:
NRCan's Keeping the Heat In ↗ estimates that a family of four generates about 50 litres (L) of water a week through normal household activities. Its weekly breakdown:

  • Breathing and skin evaporation: 38.0 L
  • Cooking three meals a day: 6.3 L
  • Bathing: 2.4 L (about 0.2 L per shower)
  • Washing clothes: 1.8 L
  • Mopping 9.3 m² (100 sq ft) of floor: 1.3 L

Other sources can add more: groundwater wicking through a foundation, small plumbing leaks, firewood stored indoors, humidifiers, houseplants and new building materials. Health Canada ↗ notes that hanging wet laundry indoors can also raise indoor humidity.

Moisture moves through a house in two ways. It diffuses slowly through materials such as drywall, and it rides along with air leaking through gaps. NRCan says one small air leak can let in 100 times more moisture than diffusion through the same area. That is why its guide calls for both a vapour barrier, to slow diffusion, and an air barrier that is continuous and well sealed, to stop moisture carried by leaking air.

sections.h2: How much humidity is right in winter
sections.html:
Relative humidity (RH) is the amount of water vapour in the air compared with the most the air could hold at that temperature. Warm air holds far more than cold air, so when room air touches cold glass it cools to its dew point and water condenses.

Health Canada recommends keeping indoor RH between 30% and 50%. NRCan adds that humidity above 20% helps prevent dry, sore throats, while higher levels can cause frosting and fogging of windows, staining, peeling paint, mould and odours. In cold weather, aim low: CMHC ↗ recommends 30% to 50% during the heating season to prevent window condensation, and 30% when it is colder than −10°C (14°F) outside.

NRCan's window table ↗ shows the highest indoor RH, with the house at 21°C, before condensation forms on the glass. Low-e glass has a thin, transparent metal coating that cuts heat loss.

A hygrometer, a small humidity meter, gives you the number. CMHC suggests checking its accuracy once a year: seal it in a plastic bag with a cup holding about 125 mL of table salt and 50 mL of water. After 8 to 12 hours it should read about 75%.

• Condensation or frost that keeps forming on the inside of windows. NRCan says occasional condensation is not a problem; excessive condensation means you should cut moisture or increase ventilation.
  • Staining or mould in bathrooms and closets, or on walls and ceilings along exterior walls.
  • A stuffy, musty smell or odours that linger.
  • In the basement: efflorescence (a whitish mineral deposit), blistering or peeling paint, crumbling concrete surfaces or a musty smell.
  • The opposite problem: static shocks, chapped lips and a scratchy throat. CMHC links very dry winter air to cold, dry air leaking in from outside.

Health Canada says mould will begin to grow within 48 hours in an area with excessive moisture. It considers an area of 1 m² or less small enough to clean yourself with proper procedures and protective equipment, and recommends that a qualified professional assess and clean up any single patch larger than 3 m². If you smell mould but can't find it, see mould and indoor air quality testing and our guide to window condensation and musty air.

An energy advisor certified by NRCan evaluates the house from the attic to the foundation, including a blower door test that measures airtightness (NRCan ↗). For moisture problems, three parts of an assessment matter most:

  • Air leaks. The blower door depressurizes the house, and an infrared camera used at the same time shows where air is leaking and insulation is missing. See thermal imaging.
  • Ventilation against moisture load. A ventilation and humidity assessment checks whether bathroom and kitchen fans actually exhaust outdoors and whether air exchange suits the number of occupants. Health Canada ↗ recommends measuring airtightness before adding a ventilation system, because the result helps pick the right one.
  • Combustion safety. NRCan notes that tightening a house raises humidity and leaves less air for fuel-burning appliances. If you have a chimney-vented furnace, water heater or fireplace, include a combustion safety test in the plan.

NRCan's first step for high humidity or condensation is to reduce the water vapour going into the air. If windows still run with water after that, increase ventilation.

• Fans that vent into the attic. Health Canada says bathroom fans must vent outside, not into the attic, and the National Building Code ↗ bars exhaust ducts from discharging into enclosed spaces.
  • Insulating a damp basement from the inside. NRCan warns not to insulate basement walls that show leaks, dampness, efflorescence or blistering paint from the inside until the moisture is corrected, or the new walls will rot (NRCan, Section 6 ↗).
  • Air sealing with no ventilation plan. Tightening raises indoor humidity. If moisture sources can't be reduced, NRCan says any retrofit that makes the house more airtight has to include mechanical ventilation.
  • Expecting new windows to fix a humidity problem. Better glazing tolerates more humidity before it fogs, as the table above shows, but it does nothing to reduce the moisture being produced.
  • Running a humidifier without checking. CMHC warns that humidifiers that are not installed, used and maintained properly can become sources of excess moisture and mould.
  • Dropping the heat too low in an empty house. NRCan advises against going below 17°C because of the risk of moisture build-up in exterior walls.

Rebates for air sealing, insulation and ventilation vary by province and change often. Check what is available where you live in our rebate program tracker, estimate the return on an upgrade with the upgrade payback calculator, and use the home energy planner to put moisture fixes in the right order before insulation.

For a damp basement, start with our guide to a cold, damp basement and NRCan's simple test: tape a 1 m (40 in.) square of plastic to the wall or slab and check it after a day or two. Condensation on top means the indoor air is humid. Condensation underneath means moisture is moving up from the ground, which NRCan says can also point to possible radon entry; see radon testing.

faq.q: What humidity should my house be in winter in Canada?
faq.a: Health Canada recommends 30% to 50%. In cold weather stay toward the low end: CMHC suggests about 30% when it is colder than −10°C outside, and NRCan's table shows ordinary double-glazed windows start to condense at about 34% when it is −20°C.

faq.q: Why do my windows get condensation on the inside in winter?
faq.a: Warm indoor air cools when it touches cold glass and drops its moisture once it reaches the dew point. Too much indoor moisture, too little ventilation or cold glass, often in combination, are the usual causes.

faq.q: How long should I run the bathroom fan after a shower?
faq.a: Health Canada says to keep it running for at least 30 minutes after a shower or bath. The fan must vent outdoors, not into the attic.

faq.q: Is it bad to dry clothes inside in winter?
faq.a: If humidity or condensation is a problem, yes. NRCan lists avoiding indoor laundry drying among the first steps, and Health Canada notes that wet laundry raises indoor humidity; a dryer vented outdoors avoids it.

faq.q: Can I clean mould myself?
faq.a: Health Canada considers an area of 1 m² or less small enough to clean yourself with proper procedures and protective equipment. A single patch larger than 3 m² should be assessed and cleaned up by a qualified professional.

faq.q: Does my basement need a dehumidifier?
faq.a: If it feels damp or you see condensation on cold surfaces, Health Canada recommends running one with the windows closed and the drain pan emptied or piped to a drain. NRCan's plastic-sheet test shows whether the moisture is coming through the foundation.

title: Home ventilation: fans and makeup air
h1: Ventilation management: fresh air, safely, in a tighter house
description: Why airtight homes need mechanical ventilation, the fan sizes Canada's building code sets, how long to run bath fans, and when you need makeup air.
blurb: Code fan sizes, how long to run them, and when a tighter house needs makeup air.
lede: Health Canada notes that construction improvements have cut unintentional air leakage areas by up to 90%, so drafts can no longer be counted on for fresh air. Ventilation guidelines call for about 5 to 10 litres per second of outdoor air per person, roughly one complete air change every three hours.

stats.label: Outdoor air per occupant in ventilation guidelines
Minimum bathroom fan rating in the National Building Code (kitchens: 50 L/s)
House depressurization that can make chimney-vented appliances backdraft

sections.h2: Why tighter houses need planned ventilation
sections.html:
Older houses got fresh air by accident, through gaps. NRCan explains that this leakage depends on wind and the indoor-outdoor temperature difference, so it peaks on cold, windy days, falls off in summer and does not reach closed bedrooms evenly. As NRCan's Keeping the Heat In ↗ puts it, “Air leakage does not make for good ventilation.”

As houses get tighter, that accidental supply shrinks. Health Canada ↗ notes that construction improvements have reduced unintentional leakage areas by up to 90% in recent decades, and that tighter houses are likely to be under-ventilated unless a mechanical system is present. The National Building Code (NBC) has called for mechanical ventilation in all new houses since its 1985 edition, which set a rate of 0.5 air changes per hour; the 1990 edition changed it to 0.3.

How much is enough? Health Canada says guidelines generally call for about 5 to 10 litres per second (L/s) of outdoor air for each occupant, or roughly a complete house air change every three hours. NRCan's target is similar: a system able to change all the household air once every three hours, plus a separate supply of combustion air for fuel-burning appliances.

sections.h2: Fans: code minimums and how long to run them
sections.html:
For houses with five or fewer bedrooms, the National Building Code 2025 ↗ describes three parts: a principal ventilation fan, supplemental exhaust fans in kitchens and bathrooms, and protection against depressurization. Provinces adopt the national code on their own schedule and sometimes change it, so check local rules. The principal fan's normal operating capacity is set by the number of bedrooms:

BedroomsMinimumMaximum
116 L/s24 L/s
218 L/s28 L/s
322 L/s32 L/s
426 L/s38 L/s
530 L/s45 L/s
  • Principal fan: approved for continuous operation, with a manual switch in the living area marked “VENTILATION FAN”. The exhaust side of an HRV can serve as this fan.
  • Bathrooms: a fan rated at least 25 L/s (about 50 cubic feet per minute, or cfm) unless the principal fan already draws from that room. Fans mounted at the ceiling or wall are capped at 2.5 sones on the CSA scale or 3.5 on the HVI scale. A sone is a loudness rating; lower is quieter.
  • Kitchens: a fan rated at least 50 L/s, ducted directly outdoors in non-combustible, corrosion-resistant duct, with a grease filter.
  • Clothes dryers: exhaust directly outdoors.

Installed fans only help when they run. Health Canada's review found that bathroom fans operate under 30 minutes a day on average, and range hoods 15 to 45 minutes. Its advice: run the bathroom fan during every shower or bath and for at least 30 minutes afterward, and use the range hood whenever you cook, preferably on the highest setting.

NRCan adds that noisy fans tend not to be used, so buy quiet ENERGY STAR certified models designed for continuous use, make sure every fan exhausts fully outdoors, and avoid range hoods that recirculate air back into the room. For a fan meant to run continuously, NRCan's ventilation fact sheet ↗ suggests one using less than 25 watts, rated 1.0 sone or less, moving 25 L/s (50 cfm). A timer or humidity control can switch a bathroom fan on and off automatically.

sections.h2: Makeup air, backdrafting and signs of trouble
sections.html:
Every litre of air a fan pushes out has to be replaced. Without a planned supply, the house is depressurized and air is pulled in through any opening, including a chimney. Health Canada notes that depressurization of around 5 pascals (Pa) can make appliances that vent through a chimney, such as open fireplaces and natural-draft water heaters, backdraft. It adds that fans larger than roughly 90 to 180 L/s (200 to 400 cfm) need added venting or ductwork to supply makeup air.

The NBC's explanatory notes name naturally aspirated gas furnaces with draft hoods, oil furnaces with barometric dampers and almost all fireplaces as susceptible to spillage. In a home with a fuel-fired furnace, boiler or water heater that is not direct-vented or mechanically vented, the code requires every exhaust device other than the principal fan to have a makeup-air fan that switches on with it and supplies at least as much outdoor air as the device exhausts, but no more than 10% extra. A depressurization test to the CAN/CGSB-51.71 standard can show that it is not needed, and the need disappears if those appliances are replaced with spillage-resistant types.

Signs of trouble. NRCan links stuffy air, lingering odours and high humidity in fall and winter to inadequate ventilation. Signs of combustion problems include soot or staining around a furnace, boiler or water heater; melted plastic fittings on top of a tank water heater; odours or hot, muggy air near the appliance; frequent headaches or nausea; and unexplained carbon monoxide alarms. If you notice any of these, book a combustion safety test and check that your carbon monoxide alarms work. If a CO alarm sounds, Health Canada ↗ says to leave immediately and call 9-1-1 from outside.

• Airtightness, with a blower door test. Health Canada recommends measuring it before adding a ventilation system, since the result helps choose the system and predict whether depressurization could become a concern.
  • Fan performance, during a ventilation assessment: whether bathroom and kitchen fans actually move air outdoors, and whether air exchange suits the number of occupants.
  • Depressurization and spillage, in a combustion safety test that checks whether exhaust devices can pull combustion gases back into the house. NRCan ↗ notes that many air-sealing companies also test ventilation and combustion air needs, including backdrafting.

For design and installation, HRAI certifies people in residential ventilation to Section 9.32 of the building code (RV9.32), design to CSA F326 (RVF326), HRV and ERV installation and balancing (VIBF) and depressurization testing (DTRS). Its certification database ↗ lets you check a name.

• Treating a bathroom fan as whole-house ventilation. NRCan says relying on a bathroom fan alone is not an effective strategy: it depends on outdoor air leaking in through random gaps.
  • Adding a powerful range hood or downdraft cooktop without makeup air in a house with a chimney-vented furnace or water heater. CMHC ↗ warns against combinations such as a natural-draft furnace with a range-top barbecue exhaust fan, and against running several powerful exhaust devices at once.
  • Ending exhaust ducts in the attic. The NBC says exhaust ducts may not discharge into heated or unheated enclosed spaces.
  • Switching ventilation off in winter. Health Canada says that in newer houses the system should run continuously at low to medium capacity for most of the year.
  • Under-ventilating a new or renovated house. NRCan calls for high ventilation rates in the first fall and winter to clear construction moisture, and during drywalling, painting or floor refinishing.

NRCan describes attention to controllable whole-house ventilation and combustion-air supply as an important part of comprehensive air sealing. If you are planning air sealing, ask for a ventilation and combustion safety check in the same visit.

Rebates vary by province and change often. Check current offers in our rebate program tracker, estimate the return on an upgrade with the upgrade payback calculator, and use the home energy planner to sequence ventilation with air sealing and heating upgrades.

faq.q: Does an older house need mechanical ventilation?
faq.a: Often, especially after air sealing. NRCan says bedrooms in older homes are often under-ventilated, recommends bathroom and kitchen fans that vent outside as a minimum, and notes that a whole-house system is more effective.

faq.q: What size bathroom fan do I need?
faq.a: The National Building Code sets a minimum of 25 L/s (about 50 cfm) where the main ventilation fan does not already draw from the bathroom. Choose a quiet one, since NRCan notes noisy fans tend not to get used.

faq.q: How long should a bathroom fan run after a shower?
faq.a: At least 30 minutes, according to Health Canada. A timer or humidity control makes that automatic.

faq.q: Do I need makeup air for my range hood?
faq.a: If the house has a furnace, boiler or water heater that vents through a chimney, the National Building Code requires a makeup-air fan for exhaust devices other than the principal ventilation fan. Health Canada also notes that fans larger than roughly 90 to 180 L/s (200 to 400 cfm) need added makeup air.

faq.q: Are recirculating range hoods enough?
faq.a: NRCan advises avoiding range hoods that recirculate air back into the room. The building code requires kitchen exhaust ducting to lead directly outdoors.

faq.q: Can I just open a window instead of running a fan?
faq.a: Occasionally, but Health Canada notes that ventilating only by opening windows can lead to excessive energy costs and makes humidity harder to manage in winter and summer.

title: HRV vs ERV: how heat recovery works
h1: HRVs and ERVs: fresh air that keeps most of the heat
description: How HRVs and ERVs work, the efficiency ratings to compare, which suits your climate, how balancing works and the maintenance schedule NRCan recommends.
blurb: How heat recovery ventilators work, which ratings to compare and how to keep them balanced.
lede: A heat recovery ventilator (HRV) replaces stale indoor air with fresh outdoor air and, according to NRCan, typically recovers 70 to 80% of the heat from the air it exhausts. An energy recovery ventilator (ERV) does the same and also moves some moisture between the airstreams.

stats.label: Heat a typical HRV recovers from outgoing air
ENERGY STAR minimum sensible recovery efficiency at 0°C / −25°C
How often to clean HRV and ERV filters

sections.h2: How an HRV or ERV works
sections.html:
An HRV pulls stale, moist air from rooms such as the kitchen, bathrooms and laundry and sends it outdoors, while bringing in the same amount of fresh outdoor air. The two airstreams pass each other in a heat-exchange core without mixing, and heat moves from the warm outgoing air to the cold incoming air. In summer the process reverses and some heat is kept out (NRCan HRV guide ↗).

NRCan's Keeping the Heat In ↗ says a typical HRV recovers 70 to 80% of the heat from the exhaust air; NRCan's ventilation fact sheet ↗ gives a range of 60 to 90% across models. An energy recovery ventilator (ERV) is a type of HRV that exchanges moisture as well as heat.

Fresh air reaches rooms through the furnace ducts or through dedicated ducts. With furnace ducts, the furnace fan has to run for the air to circulate, and Health Canada ↗ notes that an older furnace fan can draw 500 to 800 watts, compared with the 30 W fan motor in the most efficient HRVs. NRCan says a brushless DC (ECM) furnace motor can cut average furnace electricity use by more than 70% in continuous circulation, and that an HRV with its own ducts can be the most efficient setup, especially in a house without ductwork.

sections.h2: Ratings, sizing, and HRV versus ERV
sections.html:
Two ratings, both measured to the CSA C439 test standard, tell you how good a unit is:

  • Sensible recovery efficiency (SRE): the share of heat recovered after accounting for fan energy, air leakage, frost control and other losses. ENERGY STAR certification in Canada (Version 2.3 ↗, effective December 13, 2021) requires at least 65% SRE at 0°C and 60% at −25°C.
  • Fan efficacy: airflow per watt of fan power. ENERGY STAR requires at least 1.2 cfm per watt (0.57 L/s per watt) for units under 75% SRE, and 0.8 cfm per watt (0.38 L/s per watt) at 75% SRE or higher.

NRCan suggests choosing an ENERGY STAR model or one with Home Ventilating Institute (HVI) certification, with a high SRE and a low-energy fan motor. For an ERV, make sure it was tested at low temperature; all ENERGY STAR models are. Rated units are listed in NRCan's searchable product list ↗ and the HVI directory.

For sizing, NRCan's HRV guide allows 10 L/s (20 cfm) for the master bedroom, 10 L/s for an unfinished basement and 5 L/s (10 cfm) for each other room. A ten-room home works out to 60 L/s (120 cfm) at high speed, and low speed should be 40 to 60% of that.

HRV or ERV? NRCan recommends an ERV where cooling loads are high, where indoor moisture levels are very low, or in very dry climates such as northern Canada. Health Canada adds that an ERV can be the better choice for a house that is already dry in winter, and is preferable to an HRV for avoiding excess indoor humidity in summer. An HRV sends more of the winter moisture outdoors, which helps where windows sweat. If an HRV leaves the house too dry, NRCan says over-ventilation may be the cause; try a lower speed before changing equipment. Some HRVs can be converted to ERVs for less than a new unit.

An HRV is meant to move the same amount of air in as out. NRCan's guide explains that an unbalanced system recovers less heat and causes problems either way. More air out than in depressurizes the house, which can pull carbon monoxide and other combustion gases from a furnace, water heater or fireplace back indoors. More air in than out pushes moist indoor air into walls and the roof, where it can condense, and can frost the core.

The National Building Code 2025 ↗ requires installers to follow the manufacturer's start-up procedures, including air balancing and airflow measurement. NRCan recommends a balance check by a qualified contractor once a year, and a service with a balance test when you buy a home that already has an HRV.

For a rough check, CMHC ↗ suggests taping a large garbage bag to a coat hanger, holding it flat over the outdoor exhaust hood and timing how long it takes to inflate, then holding the inflated bag over the supply hood and timing how long it takes to deflate. The times should be roughly equal; if the bag inflates twice as fast as it deflates, the unit is unbalanced.

Warning signs from NRCan's troubleshooting guide:

  • Little or no airflow at the grilles: blocked hoods, dirty filters, a frozen core or loose ducts.
  • A core that keeps freezing. Most HRVs defrost automatically when incoming air is colder than −5°C, so repeated freezing points to dirty filters, a defrost fault or imbalance.
  • Cold drafts near supply grilles, wet duct insulation or water on the floor.
  • Stale air or condensing windows, or the reverse, air that is too dry in winter.

sections.h2: When you need one, and what an energy advisor checks
sections.html:
NRCan's rule: if a house already shows excessive condensation and the moisture sources can't be reduced, any retrofit that makes it more airtight has to include mechanical ventilation. It calls an energy-efficient HRV or ERV one of the best ways to ventilate a home. Health Canada notes that some jurisdictions require HRVs in new construction, while balanced and exhaust-only systems may be allowed in retrofits.

  • Airtightness: a blower door test measures it, and Health Canada says the result helps determine which ventilation system best fits the house.
  • Actual airflow: a ventilation assessment checks whether fans and any existing HRV move air outdoors as they should.
  • Pressure safety: a combustion safety test confirms an unbalanced system or exhaust fan isn't depressurizing the house around fuel-burning appliances.

For installation, NRCan recommends a contractor trained through HRAI (the Heating, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Institute of Canada) or, in Quebec, the CMMTQ. HRAI certifies HRV and ERV installation and balancing (VIBF).

sections.html:

• Turning it off. NRCan's ENERGY STAR guidance ↗ says never to turn an HRV or ERV off except for servicing. Low speed year-round usually meets ventilation needs; use high speed for cooking, showers or a full house.
  • Counting on it for combustion air. NRCan cautions not to rely on an HRV to remove combustion by-products or to supply combustion air for fuel-burning appliances.
  • Using the wrong filters. Filters not designed for your unit can restrict airflow and impair operation.
  • Expecting an air cleaner. NRCan says an HRV is not an air cleaner and may not handle strong pollutant sources such as smelly glues.
  • Covering the hoods with fine mesh. NRCan says screen mesh finer than about 6 mm (¼ in.) blocks airflow. Keep garbage, pesticides and the barbecue away from the intake.
  • Skipping commissioning. NRCan notes that historically many HRVs and ERVs were not installed or maintained properly, and says they must be installed, balanced and commissioned by a certified technician.

Rebates vary by province and change often. Check current offers in our rebate program tracker, estimate the payback with the upgrade payback calculator, and use the home energy planner to sequence ventilation with air sealing. To find someone to measure your current airflow, see our ventilation assessment providers.

faq.q: What is the difference between an HRV and an ERV?
faq.a: Both replace stale indoor air with fresh outdoor air and recover heat from the outgoing air. An ERV also transfers some moisture, so it keeps more humidity indoors in a dry winter and keeps some out in a humid summer.

faq.q: Should an HRV run all the time?
faq.a: Yes. NRCan's ENERGY STAR guidance says not to turn an HRV or ERV off except for servicing; continuous low speed usually meets ventilation needs, with high speed for showers, cooking or a full house.

faq.q: How often should I clean my HRV filters?
faq.a: Every one to three months, according to NRCan. Inspect and clean the core and condensate drain about every six months, and book a professional service once a year.

faq.q: Why does my HRV core freeze?
faq.a: Most HRVs defrost automatically when incoming air is colder than −5°C. Repeated freezing usually points to dirty filters, a defrost problem or an unbalanced system that a contractor needs to adjust.

faq.q: Do I need an HRV in an older house?
faq.a: Not always. NRCan says that if a house shows excessive condensation that can't be fixed by reducing moisture sources, any retrofit that makes it more airtight has to include mechanical ventilation.

faq.q: What efficiency rating should I look for?
faq.a: Compare the sensible recovery efficiency (SRE) at 0°C and −25°C. ENERGY STAR models sold in Canada must reach at least 65% and 60%, and a higher number means more heat recovered.

title: Heating systems: efficiency and lifespan
h1: Heating systems and controls: how each one performs
description: Gas, oil, electric baseboard, heat pumps, geothermal, wood and outdoor boilers compared by efficiency and lifespan, plus controls and when to replace.
blurb: Furnaces, boilers, baseboards, heat pumps and wood compared by efficiency and lifespan.
lede: In 2023, 23% of Canadian households heated mainly with electric baseboards and 8% with a heat pump, while wood, oil and propane each heated about 2%, so gas furnaces are only part of the picture. Here is how each system performs, what an advisor checks and when to act.

sections.h2: How it works: efficiency in plain numbers
sections.html:
Fuel-burning equipment is rated by AFUE (annual fuel utilization efficiency): the share of the fuel's energy that becomes heat in your home over a whole season. Heat pump efficiency is expressed as COP (coefficient of performance): a COP of 3 means 3 kWh of heat for every 1 kWh of electricity.

Furnaces and boilers

  • Gas furnaces from around 1970 ran at about 60% AFUE, mid-1980s models at 78–84%, and condensing furnaces 90–98% (NRCan ↗). Gas and propane furnaces made since July 3, 2019 must reach at least 95% (regulations ↗).
  • NRCan estimates that replacing a 78% furnace with a 95% model cuts annual energy costs by about 18%.
  • New hot-water gas boilers (made since July 1, 2023) must reach 90% AFUE (NRCan ↗). A condensing boiler only reaches its rating when water returns at 45–50°C or cooler; otherwise it performs like an 82–89% non-condensing boiler.
  • New oil furnaces must reach 83% AFUE and new hot-water oil boilers 86% (NRCan ↗). Oil equipment needs yearly cleaning and tuning; gas and propane equipment, servicing at least every two years (NRCan ↗).

Electric heat and heat pumps

  • Electric baseboards and electric furnaces turn all of their electricity into heat. Baseboards, used in most electrically heated Canadian homes, usually cost least to install but often have very high operating costs (NRCan ↗).
  • Air-source heat pumps deliver a COP of 2.0–5.4 at 8°C, falling to 1.1–3.7 at −8°C. Newer models stop between −15°C and −25°C, so backup heat is needed (NRCan ↗).
  • Ground-source (geothermal) heat pumps use steadier ground temperatures for a COP of about 3 in the coldest months and cut heating costs by about 65% compared with an electric furnace.
  • A dual-fuel (biénergie) system pairs a heat pump with a furnace or boiler. Below a set outdoor temperature the furnace takes over; the two don't run at the same time. Hydro-Québec's dual-energy Rate DT requires automatic switching at −12°C or −15°C, depending on the region (Hydro-Québec ↗).

sections.h2: Wood, pellets and outdoor wood boilers
sections.html:
Wood or pellets are the main heat source in about 2% of Canadian homes (Statistics Canada ↗). Efficiency and smoke depend on the appliance.

  • Look for certification. Appliances certified clean-burning by the US EPA (or to the similar CSA B415.1 standard) cut smoke by as much as 90%, and advanced stoves average about one-third more efficient than conventional ones (CMHC ↗). In British Columbia, retailers may only sell CSA- or EPA-certified appliances.
  • Compare overall efficiency. Ads often quote combustion efficiency; overall efficiency, the heat that reaches your rooms, may be 10% to 20% lower. The EPA's certified list has shown overall efficiency for every model since May 16, 2020 (US EPA ↗).
  • Burn dry wood. Aim for 20% moisture or less: split the wood, stack it off the ground, cover the top, and season softwood at least 6 months and hardwood 12.
  • Inspect every year. NRCan advises yearly stove and chimney inspections. WETT (Wood Energy Technology Transfer) says its basic (Level 1) inspection by a WETT-certified professional is used for most insurance and real estate needs (WETT ↗).

Outdoor wood boilers sit up to 40 m from the house and pipe hot water to it. Older designs produced large smoke plumes at efficiencies as low as 40%, and many municipalities restrict where they can go (CMHC). In BC, new outdoor wood boilers must be at least 40 m from adjacent property lines (10 m for pellet boilers) (B.C. ↗). In Ontario, rules are local: North Dundas requires a certified unit, a permit, 30 m from any property line and 100 m from a neighbour's house, and bans them in subdivisions and residential zones (by-law ↗). Check with your municipality first.

Minimums are from current NRCan regulations. Other ranges come from NRCan and CMHC guides; the figures for wood, pellets and older gas equipment date from NRCan's 2012 Heating with Gas guide.
