sections.h2: Controls and free heat from the sun
sections.html:
• Programmable or smart thermostats. Lowering the temperature 1°C for eight hours saves about 2% of heating energy. Don't go below 17°C, which risks moisture in exterior walls (NRCan ↗); ENERGY STAR Canada suggests 17°C asleep or away and 20°C at home (ENERGY STAR ↗).
  • Heat pumps. Keep setbacks to 2°C or less (or use a smart thermostat that recovers early), and set electric backup 2–3°C below the heat pump setting (NRCan).
  • Electric baseboards. Electronic thermostats that hold within 0.5°C of the setting could save about 3% (NRCan).
  • Zones. Radiator valves or duct dampers with their own thermostats let you heat rooms differently.

Passive solar gain is free heat through your windows. A window's solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC, from 0 to 1) shows how much of the sun's heat it lets in. NRCan suggests above 0.4 for pre-1980 or poorly sealed homes, passive solar designs and sunny areas with short cooling seasons, and 0.3–0.4 for new or substantially renovated homes. Curtains and blinds cut heat loss through glass in winter and block summer sun (NRCan ↗).

sections.h2: When to repair, replace or switch
sections.html:
Hydro One says a furnace can work reliably for 15 to 20 years, likely longer if maintained. Warning signs: frequent repairs, rising bills at the same setting, popping, banging or screeching, and dust or soot around registers. It suggests replacing a furnace over 15 years old when repairs would cost 50% or more of a new high-efficiency unit (Hydro One ↗).

Call a technician promptly about signs of combustion trouble: soot or staining around a burner, damper or vent connection, melted plastic fittings on top of a tank water heater, unusual odours, frequent headaches or nausea, or carbon monoxide alarms. Building codes now require a CO alarm in every home with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage (NRCan). See combustion safety testing.

Air-source heat pumps last 15–20 years and ground-source units 20–25. When a central air conditioner needs replacing, NRCan notes a heat pump often costs little more; see thinking about a heat pump. After insulation and air sealing, a furnace may be oversized and short-cycle; staged and modulating furnaces fire at 60–100% of capacity for steadier cycles (NRCan).

In an EnerGuide evaluation, the advisor records the size and efficiency ratings of your heating, cooling and water heating equipment, photographs mechanical systems and any wood-burning appliances, and measures airtightness with a blower door test. Fuel-fired heating is turned down during the test because the fan can affect safe operation of gas appliances (NRCan ↗).

NRCan advises sealing air leaks and insulating before choosing a heat pump, because a tighter house can use a smaller unit. Equipment should be sized with a recognized load calculation such as CSA F280 (see heat loss calculation), and an all-electric air-source or ground-source heat pump normally needs a 200-amp electrical service.

sections.h2: Mistakes to avoid and next steps
sections.html:
• Replacing like for like without a load calculation: oversized equipment short-cycles or runs inefficiently, and an undersized heat pump leans on backup heat.
  • Counting on an open fireplace for heat: NRCan says most can't provide any net heat gain.
  • Deep setbacks with a heat pump, which bring on backup heat.
  • Letting a door-to-door “inspector” in: NRCan and its programs never perform or authorize unsolicited inspections (NRCan ↗).

Next steps: check rebates where you live on our programs page, compare running costs with the energy cost calculator, and put upgrades in order with the planner.

faq.q: Is electric baseboard heating inefficient?
faq.a: Baseboards turn all of their electricity into heat, but NRCan notes they often have very high operating costs. A heat pump moves heat instead of making it, delivering about 2 to 5 units of heat per unit of electricity in mild weather.

faq.q: Do heat pumps work in a Canadian winter?
faq.a: Yes, with limits. Newer air-source models keep running down to somewhere between −15°C and −25°C and lose efficiency as it gets colder, so a backup heat source is needed. Ground-source systems keep working whatever the outdoor temperature.

faq.q: Are outdoor wood boilers allowed where I live?
faq.a: It depends on your province and municipality. BC requires new outdoor wood boilers to be at least 40 m from adjacent property lines, and many municipalities restrict where they can go, so check with your local building department before buying.

faq.q: How much can a programmable thermostat save?
faq.a: NRCan estimates about 2% of heating energy for each 1°C you lower the temperature over eight hours. Don't go below 17°C, and keep heat pump setbacks to 2°C or less.

faq.q: When should I replace my furnace?
faq.a: Hydro One says furnaces typically last 15 to 20 years. It suggests replacing one that is over 15 years old and needs repairs costing half or more of a new high-efficiency unit.

faq.q: What is a dual-fuel heating system?
faq.a: A heat pump paired with a furnace or boiler. The heat pump handles milder weather and the furnace takes over below a set outdoor temperature; the two don't run at the same time.

title: Thermostat setbacks and settings that save
h1: Thermostat management: setbacks, smart controls and humidity
description: NRCan's setback savings figure, the 17°C and 20°C schedule, how to handle heat pumps and baseboards, plus zoning, smart thermostats and humidistats.
blurb: What a setback saves, the 17°C and 20°C schedule, and how heat pumps and baseboards differ.
lede: NRCan says a drop of 1°C over eight hours can save about 2% of heating energy. Yet in 2023 only about half of Canadian households with a thermostat turned it down while they slept.

stats.label: Heating energy saved for each 1°C of setback held for 8 hours
NRCan's suggested settings: asleep or away / awake and home
of households with a thermostat turned it down while asleep in winter (2023)

sections.html:
NRCan's wording in Keeping the Heat In ↗: “A drop of 1°C (2°F) over an eight-hour period can save about 2 percent on your heating energy consumption.” It adds that turning the heat down is worthwhile whenever you are away for more than three or four hours, and that a basic programmable thermostat should allow at least two setback periods a day, for example one overnight and one while everyone is out.

How far? The ENERGY STAR guidance NRCan publishes for smart thermostats ↗ says lowering the temperature 2°C to 3°C is optimal, and suggests 17°C when you are sleeping or out and 20°C when you are home and awake. NRCan advises against going below 17°C in general because of the risk of moisture build-up in exterior walls; for absences of a week or more, keep indoor humidity low if you set it lower. NRCan also notes that space heating and cooling make up almost two-thirds of home energy use.

Most Canadians have the equipment but don't use it fully. In Statistics Canada's 2023 Households and the Environment Survey ↗, 91% of households had at least one thermostat, and 61% of those had a programmable main thermostat, up from 42% in 2007. Yet only 51% of households with a thermostat lowered it in winter while asleep, and 43% kept it the same. Among households with a programmable thermostat, 62% turned it down at night.

sections.h2: Heat pumps, baseboards and hot-water systems
sections.html:
Heat pumps

Heat pumps respond more slowly than furnaces. NRCan's heat pump guide ↗ recommends setbacks of no more than 2°C, or a smart thermostat that switches the system on early to recover from a setback, and setting any electric backup heat 2°C to 3°C below the heat pump's set-point. After a deeper setback, the backup system may run until the heat pump catches up, which cuts into the savings. The US Department of Energy ↗ puts it plainly: don't set back a heat pump if it makes the backup heat come on. Hydro-Québec ↗ goes further and suggests keeping a heat pump at a constant temperature, for example 21°C, with baseboard heaters around 19°C.

Electric baseboards

Baseboards use line-voltage thermostats (120 or 240 volts) in each room or area, which Hydro-Québec ↗ recommends having installed by a master electrician. It estimates that replacing conventional thermostats with smart ones could save up to 10% on heating costs a year, and suggests lowering the temperature in unoccupied rooms and keeping their doors closed.

Hot-water (hydronic) systems

NRCan's setback advice excludes some hydronic systems with slow response times. For these it points to thermostat-controlled valves on each radiator, and to an outdoor reset control that adjusts the circulating water temperature to the weather.

Smart, or connected, thermostats can be adjusted from a phone and report energy use. NRCan says adaptive models, which use weather, occupancy or how close you are to home to set a schedule, provide greater savings than programmable thermostats, and that ENERGY STAR certified models have been independently certified, based on actual field data, to deliver energy savings. Hydro-Québec notes that smart thermostats work best when the temperature is kept stable rather than changed often.

Zoning gives parts of the house their own thermostats. In a forced-air system, NRCan describes dampers in the ducts controlled by separate thermostats; in a hot-water system, thermostat-controlled valves on each radiator.

A humidistat controls humidity rather than temperature, and NRCan ↗ notes it tracks humidity more accurately than watching windows. If you have a furnace humidifier or an HRV dehumidistat, adjust it with the seasons. NRCan's table, at 21°C indoors, puts the condensation limit for ordinary double-glazed windows at 44% relative humidity when it is −10°C outside and 34% at −20°C.

sections.h2: Signs of trouble and what an energy advisor checks
sections.html:
Uneven temperatures are often blamed on the thermostat when the cause is elsewhere. NRCan notes that undersized or leaky ducts and poorly placed return grilles cause discomfort and higher bills; that in summer a single main-floor thermostat can leave the second floor too warm and the basement too cold; and that a furnace left oversized after a retrofit can short-cycle and swing temperatures. On a heat pump, backup heat that comes on after every setback is another sign the settings need work.

Tests that help:

  • A 12-month bill analysis separates heating from baseload use, showing what a setback is worth in your house.
  • Blower door and thermal imaging tests locate air leaks and missing insulation.
  • Duct leakage and airflow testing shows whether some rooms are short of warm air.

• Cranking the thermostat to warm up faster. Hydro-Québec ↗ notes that setting a higher temperature than you want does not warm the house any faster.
  • Deep setbacks on a heat pump. NRCan recommends no more than 2°C, because the backup heat may run until the heat pump catches up.
  • Leaving an empty house below 17°C without watching humidity. NRCan links low settings to moisture build-up in exterior walls.
  • Constant manual changes on a smart thermostat. Hydro-Québec says they are more effective when the temperature is kept stable.
  • Running baseboards at the same set-point as a central system. Hydro-Québec suggests setting baseboards about 2°C lower so both don't run at once.
  • Throwing out an old thermostat. Some thermostats contain mercury. HRAI's Thermostat Recovery Program ↗ accepts mercury, electronic and mechanical thermostats for free.

Rebates vary by province and change often. Check current offers in our rebate program tracker, estimate the return on bigger upgrades with the upgrade payback calculator, and use the home energy planner to see where controls fit alongside air sealing and heating upgrades. If you are switching to a heat pump, ask the installer for the best backup heat set-point and setback limit for your system, as NRCan recommends.

faq.q: How much do you save by turning down the thermostat?
faq.a: NRCan says a drop of 1°C held for eight hours saves about 2% of heating energy. It adds that turning the heat down is worthwhile whenever you are away for more than three or four hours.

faq.q: What temperature should I set my thermostat at night in winter?
faq.a: NRCan's ENERGY STAR guidance suggests 17°C while you sleep or are out and 20°C when you are home and awake. NRCan advises against going below 17°C because of the risk of moisture build-up in exterior walls.

faq.q: Should I turn down my heat pump at night?
faq.a: Only slightly. NRCan recommends setbacks of no more than 2°C, or a smart thermostat that starts recovery early, so the electric backup heat doesn't come on.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to keep the heat at one temperature all day?
faq.a: With a furnace or baseboards, no: NRCan says turning the heat down is worthwhile if you are away for more than three or four hours. Heat pumps and some hot-water systems respond slowly, so keep their setbacks small.

faq.q: Do smart thermostats work with electric baseboard heaters?
faq.a: Yes, but baseboards need line-voltage (120 or 240 V) models in each room or area. Hydro-Québec recommends having them installed by a master electrician.

faq.q: What do I do with an old mercury thermostat?
faq.a: Don't put it in the garbage. HRAI's Thermostat Recovery Program accepts mercury, electronic and mechanical thermostats for recycling at no charge.

title: Furnace and heat pump maintenance
h1: HVAC maintenance: keeping furnaces, boilers and heat pumps safe and efficient
description: How often to service furnaces, boilers and heat pumps, filter and MERV advice, duct sealing, CO alarms, and what a proper tune-up should include.
blurb: How often each system needs service, what a tune-up covers and carbon monoxide safety.
lede: Health Canada advises having fuel-burning appliances professionally inspected at least once a year, and Hydro-Québec says a heat pump without proper maintenance can use up to 25% more electricity. NRCan says homeowners can handle some of the work in between.

sections.h2: How often each system needs service
sections.html:
NRCan's Keeping the Heat In ↗ says a qualified service technician should perform annual maintenance and efficiency tune-ups, and that homeowners can do some of the work in between. Intervals by system, from NRCan and Health Canada:

SystemProfessional serviceHomeowner tasks
Oil furnace or boilerCleaning and tuning every yearChange or clean the filter every 3 months, or sooner when loaded
Natural gas or propane furnace or boilerAt least every two years (NRCan minimum); Health Canada advises an inspection of fuel-burning appliances at least once a yearFilter every 3 months; keep exhaust vents clear of snow and ice
Wood stove or fireplaceInspect the equipment and chimney every year and clean as needed; Health Canada says to have a wood-burning fireplace chimney cleaned every yearKeep a CO alarm in the room; the building code requires one

Ground-source heat pumpEvery year (NRCan heat pump guide); Keeping the Heat In says at least every two yearsFilter every 3 months on air systems
Central air conditionerPeriodic service by a contractorClean or change the filter; keep the outdoor condenser clear of plants and leaves

The yearly inspection advice from Health Canada ↗ is about carbon monoxide (CO). Where intervals differ, follow the more frequent one and your manufacturer's instructions.

HRAI ↗, the Heating, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Institute of Canada, says a furnace inspection by a licensed technician should include:

  • a safety test for carbon monoxide
  • checking the chimney and flue for debris
  • cleaning and reinstalling air filters
  • checking the thermostat and safety controls, and the gas pilot safety system
  • cleaning the motor and fan, and checking blower operation (and the fan belt on older systems)
  • cleaning burners and setting them for proper combustion and ignition
  • checking the gas piping to the furnace

For heat pumps, the US Department of Energy ↗ adds measuring the refrigerant charge, checking for refrigerant leaks, measuring airflow, sealing duct leaks, tightening electrical connections, lubricating motors, and confirming that heating and cooling can't run at the same time. CMHC ↗ notes that a properly tuned combustion appliance rarely produces carbon monoxide, and suggests asking for furnace cycles of six minutes or longer to limit spillage at start-up.

To find a contractor, HRAI's Contractor Locator ↗ lists members, who must carry insurance and valid trade certificates and licences, and agree to HRAI's code of ethics.

sections.h2: Signs of trouble and carbon monoxide safety
sections.html:
• Soot or staining around a furnace, boiler or water heater, or melted plastic fittings on top of a tank water heater: signs of back-puffing, according to NRCan.
  • Unusual odours or hot, muggy air around a fuel-burning appliance.
  • Frequent headaches, skin or throat irritation or nausea, or unexplained smoke or CO alarms.
  • Exhaust vents blocked by ice or snow; Health Canada says to check them during and after snowstorms.
  • Rooms that never heat evenly, which NRCan links to undersized or leaky ducts and poorly placed return grilles.

Health Canada lists early CO symptoms as tiredness, headaches, flu-like symptoms and shortness of breath; higher levels bring dizziness, chest pain, poor vision and difficulty thinking (symptoms ↗). If a CO alarm sounds, leave the home immediately, don't try to find the source, call 9-1-1 from outside and return only after a professional has fixed the problem.

The National Building Code 2025 ↗ requires CO alarms in homes with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, certified to CSA 6.19 and placed inside each bedroom or within 5 m of each bedroom door. Health Canada says the most important spot is the hallway outside sleeping areas; test alarms regularly and replace them by the manufacturer's expiry date. See our CO alarm guide.

• Combustion safety: a combustion safety and spillage test checks whether exhaust fans can depressurize the house enough to pull flue gases back in. HRAI certifies technicians in depressurization testing (DTRS).
  • Carbon monoxide: a CO alarm check confirms your alarms meet the requirements above.
  • Ducts: duct leakage and airflow testing pressure-tests the ductwork and measures airflow at each register.
  • Sizing before replacement: NRCan notes that a house with less heat loss after retrofits needs smaller equipment, and that oversizing causes short cycling. Its heat pump guide ↗ recommends sizing to CSA F280; see our room-by-room heat loss calculation.

sections.h2: Maintenance and fixes, from simplest to biggest
sections.html:
Filters. NRCan says to change or clean forced-air filters every three months or as they become loaded; Hydro-Québec ↗ suggests checking heat pump filters monthly during heavy use. On MERV, the rating printed on the filter, CMHC ↗ says a higher number means better filtration, but some higher-MERV filters reduce airflow through the furnace and affect its performance, so ask your technician before upgrading.

Heat pumps and air conditioners. In cold weather an air-source heat pump periodically runs a defrost cycle to melt frost off its outdoor coil; that is normal. NRCan puts its service life at 15 to 20 years (20 to 25 for ground-source). Air conditioners lose efficiency when the indoor coil is dirty, the outdoor condenser is blocked or the refrigerant runs low.

• Sealing ducts with standard vinyl duct tape. NRCan says its adhesive dries out over time and the tape falls off.
  • Paying for duct cleaning to fix air quality or bills. CMHC ↗ and US EPA research found little or no difference in airborne particles or airflow after cleaning, and NRCan says it generally has little effect. CMHC also advises declining offers to spray or “fog” ducts with biocides.
  • Upgrading to a high-MERV filter without checking. Some restrict airflow through the furnace.
  • Ignoring an alarm, or hunting for the source. Leave first and call from outside.
  • Running fuel-burning equipment indoors. Health Canada says never to run a generator indoors or idle a vehicle in the garage, even with the door open.
  • Blocking airflow. NRCan warns that furniture or carpeting over vents and registers can shorten equipment life and reduce efficiency.

Rebates for heating equipment and duct work vary by province and change often. Check current offers in our rebate program tracker, estimate whether replacing equipment pays off with the upgrade payback calculator, and use the home energy planner to line up maintenance, air sealing and any equipment change in the right order.

faq.q: How often should a furnace be serviced in Canada?
faq.a: NRCan says oil furnaces need cleaning and tuning every year and gas or propane furnaces at least every two years, while recommending annual maintenance by a qualified technician. Health Canada advises a professional inspection of fuel-burning appliances at least once a year.

faq.q: How often should I change my furnace filter?
faq.a: Every three months, or sooner when it is loaded, according to NRCan. Ask your technician before switching to a higher-MERV filter, since CMHC notes some reduce airflow.

faq.q: Do heat pumps need annual maintenance?
faq.a: Yes. NRCan recommends annual maintenance by a qualified contractor plus cleaning or changing the filter every three months, and Hydro-Québec says a poorly maintained heat pump can use up to 25% more electricity.

faq.q: Is duct cleaning worth it?
faq.a: Not for air quality or energy savings in most homes. CMHC research found little or no difference in airborne particles or airflow after cleaning, though it can make sense after construction, water in the ducts or a blockage.

faq.q: Where should carbon monoxide alarms go?
faq.a: The National Building Code requires them inside each bedroom or within 5 m of each bedroom door in homes with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage. Health Canada says the most important spot is the hallway outside sleeping areas.

faq.q: What should a furnace tune-up include?
faq.a: HRAI's list includes a carbon monoxide safety test, a chimney and flue check, filter cleaning, thermostat and safety control checks, motor, fan and blower cleaning, and burner cleaning with combustion and ignition set-up.

title: Water heaters: tank, tankless and heat pump
h1: Water heaters: tank, tankless and heat pump options
description: Water heating is about 17% of home energy in Canada. Compare tank, tankless, heat pump and condensing models, safe settings, lifespans and rebates.
blurb: Tank, tankless, heat pump and condensing heaters, safe settings and when to replace.
lede: Water heating uses 17.2% of the energy in the average Canadian home, second only to space heating. The type of heater, its size and its settings decide how much of that you can save.

stats.label: of energy in the average Canadian home goes to water heating
more efficient: on-demand vs tank where daily use is 155 L or less (US DOE)
less energy for an ENERGY STAR heat pump water heater vs a standard electric tank

sections.h2: How it works: where the energy goes
sections.html:
NRCan puts water heating at 17.2% of the energy used in the average Canadian home, second only to space heating (ENERGY STAR Canada ↗). Its Keeping the Heat In guide says about 20%, and notes that in a new or deeply renovated home, water heating can use more energy than space heating (NRCan ↗). In all-electric Quebec homes, Hydro-Québec puts hot water at 16% of electricity use in a detached house and 21–22% in a plex or multi-unit building (Hydro-Québec ↗).

Canadians use an average of 75 litres of hot water each per day (ENERGY STAR Canada). NRCan's Water Heater Guide puts the average household at 225 L a day, with three people using anywhere from 110 to 450 L depending on habits and fixtures; showers and baths account for almost half (NRCan ↗).

Gas and oil water heaters are rated by energy factor (EF): the share of energy that ends up as hot water over a standard 24-hour test, including heat lost from the tank while it sits (standby loss). Electric tanks are rated by standby loss in watts. A higher EF and a lower standby loss are better.

A tank keeps water hot around the clock; a tankless (on-demand) heater heats water only as it flows. The US Department of Energy (US DOE ↗) states: “For homes that use 41 gallons or less of hot water daily, demand water heaters can be 24%–34% more energy efficient than conventional storage tank water heaters. They can be 8%–14% more energy efficient for homes that use a lot of hot water — around 86 gallons per day.” By our conversion, those thresholds are about 155 and 326 litres a day; NRCan's average household (225 L) falls between them.

ENERGY STAR Canada says a certified tankless model uses 30% less energy, on average, than a storage tank (ENERGY STAR Canada ↗). In NRCan's 2011 listings, gas tankless models had EFs of 0.64–0.98 (average 0.85), against 0.53–0.70 (average 0.62) for gas tanks.

The limits: tankless units typically deliver 7.6–15.2 litres a minute, so a shower and the dishwasher together can stretch one; a gas model with a standing pilot light gives back some of the savings, so look for intermittent ignition (US DOE). Most electric tankless units can't supply a whole house and are rarely installed that way in Canada, and NRCan notes hot water will likely take longer to reach the tap.

sections.h2: Heat pump, condensing, combi and heat recovery options
sections.html:
• Heat pump water heaters move heat from the surrounding air into the tank. ENERGY STAR Canada says certified models use up to 70% less energy than a standard electric water heater (ENERGY STAR Canada ↗); the US DOE says two to three times as efficient as conventional electric water heaters. They need a space that stays between 4.4°C and 32.2°C all year with at least 28.3 m³ of air around them, and they cool the room they're in, so a warm furnace room improves their efficiency (US DOE ↗).
  • Condensing gas water heaters, tank or tankless, use a condensing heat exchanger, similar to a high-efficiency furnace; NRCan suggests them where large amounts of hot water are needed.
  • Combination (combi) systems use one water heater or boiler for space and water heating, and suit homes that need less heat. They aren't regulated; look for a rating to CSA P.9 and a designer certified for combination systems by the Heating, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Institute of Canada (HRAI) (NRCan ↗).
  • Drain-water heat recovery coils the cold supply pipe around the drain stack so warm shower water preheats incoming water. It has no moving parts and works best when hot water drains while fresh water is drawn, as in a shower (NRCan ↗).
  • Solar water heaters can use up to 60% less energy than other water heaters and need a backup heater (NRCan ↗).

sections.h2: Settings, safety and when to replace
sections.html:
Set the tank to 60°C to prevent the growth of bacteria such as Legionella, and use mixing (anti-scald) valves to deliver 49°C at taps, showers and tubs (Public Health Agency of Canada ↗). At 60°C, water can scald in under five seconds; at 52°C it takes 1.5 to 2 minutes (NRCan). NRCan warns that lowering the tank temperature too far may promote bacterial growth, especially in electric tanks.

Storage water heaters last 10–15 years and most tankless units more than 20 (US DOE). ENERGY STAR Canada suggests upgrading a water heater more than 10 years old, and NRCan advises choosing a replacement before the old one fails, so you are not forced into a rushed decision.

On a gas or oil tank, soot or staining around the vent connection, or melted plastic fittings on top of the tank, can mean exhaust is spilling into the house (NRCan). Have it checked; see combustion safety testing.

An EnerGuide evaluation records the size and efficiency rating of your water heating equipment, and fuel-fired water heaters are turned down during the blower door test (NRCan ↗). The rating assumes standard hot water use, so your household's use may differ. Your report breaks down energy use, including water heating.

In Ontario, the Home Renovation Savings program pays $500 for replacing a gas, oil, propane or electric water heater with an ENERGY STAR heat pump water heater (as of October 2026). It counts only as one of at least two qualifying upgrades, and the initial home energy assessment must happen before any work (Home Renovation Savings ↗). See program details.

sections.h2: Mistakes to avoid and next steps
sections.html:
• Buying a bigger tank than you need: larger tanks are typically less efficient, especially when demand is low (NRCan).
  • Undersizing a tankless unit for showers and appliances running at the same time.
  • Putting a heat pump water heater in a cold or cramped space.
  • Skipping pipe insulation: insulating hot and cold pipes within 2–3 m of the heater is the most cost-effective improvement (ENERGY STAR Canada ↗); NRCan suggests at least RSI 0.7 (R-4).
  • Expecting an ENERGY STAR electric or oil tank: those types aren't eligible.

Next steps: look for water heater rebates on our programs page, compare running costs with the energy cost calculator, and fit the upgrade into your plan.

faq.q: Is a tankless water heater worth it?
faq.a: It depends on how much hot water you use. The US DOE says on-demand units are 24–34% more efficient in homes using about 155 litres a day or less, and 8–14% more efficient in homes using about 326 litres; gas models suit whole-house use better than electric ones.

faq.q: What temperature should my water heater be set to?
faq.a: The Public Health Agency of Canada recommends 60°C at the tank to prevent bacteria such as Legionella, with mixing valves limiting taps, showers and tubs to 49°C to prevent scalds.

faq.q: How long does a water heater last?
faq.a: The US DOE puts storage tanks at 10–15 years and most tankless units at more than 20. ENERGY STAR Canada suggests upgrading once a heater is more than 10 years old.

faq.q: Will a heat pump water heater make my basement cold?
faq.a: It can, because it pulls heat from the surrounding air. It needs a space that stays between 4.4°C and 32.2°C with plenty of air around it, and a warm furnace room improves its efficiency.

faq.q: How much hot water does a household use?
faq.a: About 75 litres per person per day, according to ENERGY STAR Canada. NRCan puts the average household at 225 litres a day.

title: Air conditioning: energy use and ratings
h1: Air conditioning and cooling: energy use, ratings and upkeep
description: How much electricity air conditioning uses in Canada, what SEER2, EER and CEER mean, heat pumps vs window units, shading, attic venting and upkeep.
blurb: What SEER2 and CEER mean, keeping heat out first, and upkeep that protects efficiency.
lede: 68% of Canadian households now have air conditioning or a heat pump that cools, including 83% in Ontario. Cooling is a small share of yearly energy in most homes, but it drives summer bills and peak demand, and shading and upkeep cut it.

stats.label: of Canadian households had air conditioning or a cooling heat pump in 2025 (83% in Ontario)
Minimum SEER2 for split central air conditioners made since Jan. 1, 2023
of yearly electricity use goes to cooling in all-electric Quebec homes with AC

sections.html:
Across all Canadian homes, including those without air conditioning, space cooling was 1.6% of household energy use in NRCan's 2019 breakdown (NRCan ↗). In all-electric Quebec homes that have air conditioning, Hydro-Québec puts it at about 3% of yearly electricity use, roughly 720 kWh, by our arithmetic, of the 24,000 kWh an average detached home uses (Hydro-Québec ↗).

Summer is a different story. In 2015, Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator reported that on the hottest days, increased air conditioning use accounted for roughly a third of the province's electricity use (IESO ↗). BC Hydro's 2020 data show the average central air conditioner runs 9.4 hours a day when in use, and BC Hydro estimates each degree lower on the thermostat can add 3% to cooling costs (BC Hydro, 2020 ↗).

Settings matter. In 2025, households with air conditioning set their thermostats to 21.3°C on average in the warmer months (Statistics Canada ↗), cooler than the 22–25°C NRCan suggests for central systems; NRCan's ENERGY STAR pages recommend 25–27°C. NRCan estimates a unit's seasonal use from your area's cooling degree-days and summer design temperature, the unit's capacity and its SEER. One ton of cooling capacity is 12,000 Btu/h, or 3.5 kW (NRCan, Air Conditioning Your Home ↗).

• SEER (seasonal energy efficiency ratio): cooling delivered over a season divided by the electricity used, based on a climate with a 28°C average summer temperature. Higher is better.
  • EER (energy efficiency ratio): the same idea measured at one fixed temperature, a snapshot rather than a season.
  • SEER2 and HSPF2: newer seasonal cooling and heating ratings (HSPF is the heating seasonal performance factor) calculated with a different, US-based test procedure. Don't compare a SEER2 number directly with an older SEER number (NRCan ↗).
  • CEER (combined energy efficiency ratio): the rating on the mandatory EnerGuide label for window (louvred) and through-the-wall units (NRCan ↗).

Minimums for new equipment: split-system central air conditioners made since January 1, 2023 need SEER2 13.4 (NRCan ↗); split-system heat pumps made since January 1, 2025 need SEER2 14.3 and HSPF2 6.0 (NRCan ↗); room air conditioners made from May 26, 2026 must meet new CEER minimums, for example 16.0 for an 8,000–13,999 Btu/h window unit without reverse cycle (NRCan ↗). ENERGY STAR central units use 8% less energy than standard models and room units 10% less, and replacing a central air conditioner more than 10 years old can save upwards of 30% (ENERGY STAR Canada ↗).

sections.h2: Keep the heat out first: shading, attic insulation and ventilation
sections.html:
• Shade the glass. Awnings, blinds or drapes keep direct sun out; deciduous trees on the south and west sides and wide roof overhangs cut summer sun with little effect in winter; light-coloured exterior finishes reduce solar heat gain (NRCan). BC Hydro's 2020 report says shading windows can block up to 65% of the heat (BC Hydro ↗).
  • Choose glass for your climate. Low-e coatings can cut summer heat gain by up to 50%, and a lower SHGC lets in less solar heat. Solar-control films help on problem windows but can raise heating bills if used on every window (NRCan ↗).
  • Insulate and vent the attic. Seal air leaks and insulate the attic and walls to at least recommended levels. Attic ventilation reduces summer heat build-up and air conditioner load; NRCan advises against powered attic fans, which can pull house air into the attic (NRCan ↗).
  • Time your chores. Do cooking, dishwashing, clothes drying and bathing in cooler hours, and use bathroom and range fans that exhaust outside.
  • Fix hot upper floors. Adjusting duct dampers can rebalance summer airflow; where ducts fall short, NRCan suggests a ductless mini-split upstairs (NRCan ↗). See house won't stay cool in summer.

Have a central system serviced every year, ideally just before the cooling season (NRCan; ENERGY STAR Canada). Between visits, clean or replace filters (NRCan suggests every 3 months for heat pumps and at least once a season for room units), keep the outdoor unit clear of leaves and grass clippings, and gently hose the coil after vacuuming it. Dirty filters and coils cut airflow, efficiency and capacity, and left long enough can damage the compressor. If cooling is still weak after cleaning, a contractor should check the refrigerant level.

A house that feels cool but clammy can point to an oversized unit that shuts off before removing humidity (NRCan). NRCan puts central air conditioner life at 15 years or longer; when a major part such as the compressor fails, replacing may make more sense than repairing. Removing and storing a window unit over winter extends its life (ENERGY STAR Canada ↗).

An EnerGuide evaluation records the size and efficiency rating of your cooling equipment along with airtightness, insulation and the number, type and location of windows, and your label shows how much of your home's energy goes to cooling (NRCan ↗). For new equipment, a contractor should size the unit from a cooling load calculation (NRCan points to CSA F280) that accounts for insulation and the number, type and orientation of windows; see heat loss calculation.

sections.h2: Mistakes to avoid and next steps
sections.html:
• Oversizing: a bigger unit cools too fast without drying the air, leaving the house cold and damp.
  • Single-hose portable units: they depressurize the house and draw in hot outdoor air; NRCan suggests a dual-hose model, and BC Hydro's 2020 report says portables use twice the energy of a window unit.
  • Leaving the indoor fan on “on”: SEER ratings assume “auto”, and continuous fan use adds cost and can return moisture to the air.
  • Keeping the old indoor coil with a new outdoor unit, so the system misses its rated efficiency.
  • Buying a cooling-only unit when your heating also needs work: a heat pump does both, and NRCan says the extra cost over a cooling-only system is often quite low.

Next steps: look for cooling and heat pump rebates on our programs page, estimate summer running costs with the energy cost calculator, and add shading and attic work to your plan.

faq.q: How much does air conditioning add to my electricity use?
faq.a: In all-electric Quebec homes with air conditioning, Hydro-Québec puts cooling at about 3% of yearly electricity use. It weighs more in summer: on the hottest days, air conditioning drove roughly a third of Ontario's electricity use (IESO, 2015).

faq.q: What temperature should I set my air conditioner to?
faq.a: NRCan's air conditioning booklet suggests 22–25°C for central systems, and its ENERGY STAR pages recommend 25–27°C. In 2025, the average among Canadian households with air conditioning was 21.3°C, below both.

faq.q: Is a heat pump better than a central air conditioner?
faq.a: For cooling they are similar, but a heat pump also heats. NRCan says the extra cost over a cooling-only system is often quite low, and new split heat pumps must meet a higher SEER2 minimum (14.3) than central air conditioners (13.4).

faq.q: Are portable air conditioners efficient?
faq.a: Generally not. NRCan says single-hose units draw hot outdoor air into the house and suggests a dual-hose model, and BC Hydro's 2020 report says portables use about twice the energy of a window unit.

faq.q: How often should my air conditioner be serviced?
faq.a: Once a year, ideally just before the cooling season, with filters and the outdoor coil cleaned more often (NRCan, ENERGY STAR Canada).

faq.q: Why is my upstairs so hot in summer?
faq.a: Upper floors get more sun, warm air rises, and ducts are usually designed for heating. Rebalancing the dampers can help, and where ducts fall short NRCan suggests a ductless mini-split upstairs.

title: EnerGuide home ratings explained
h1: EnerGuide ratings: what the number means and how to get one
description: What an EnerGuide rating in gigajoules means, how to read the label and upgrade report, who can do an evaluation, how long it takes and what it costs.
blurb: What the gigajoule number means, how to read the label and what an evaluation costs.
lede: An EnerGuide rating estimates how much energy your house uses in a year under standard conditions, in gigajoules (GJ). The average Canadian household uses about 100 GJ a year; lower is better, and zero means the house produces as much energy as it uses.

stats.label: Average yearly energy use of a Canadian household
NRCan's average for pre- and post-retrofit evaluations together (as of October 2026)
for an initial evaluation; about 1 hour for the follow-up (Ontario program)

sections.html:
An energy advisor measures your home and enters the data into HOT2000, NRCan's energy simulation software, which calculates the rating (NRCan ↗). One gigajoule is roughly the energy to run a typical fridge for 30 weeks.

  • Net energy in GJ per year. The scale runs toward zero; a home rated 0 GJ produces as much energy as it consumes (NRCan ↗).
  • Reference house. Each rated home gets its own reference: the same house as if built to typical new-construction standards, so you can see how far yours is from a new home (NRCan ↗).
  • Standard operating conditions. The software assumes standard thermostat settings, hot water use and number of occupants, so the rating applies to the house, not your household. NRCan says your bills shouldn't be expected to match it, and large extra loads such as a pool or hot tub are listed separately as “atypical energy loads”.
  • Old 0–100 scale. NRCan retired the 0–100 scale at the end of 2018; since January 1, 2019, all new evaluations use GJ per year, and old ratings can't be converted.

After the visit you receive three documents (NRCan ↗):

  1. EnerGuide label: your rating as a number and on the GJ scale, energy use by source, how you compare with your reference house, the share going to heating, cooling, ventilation and other uses, and your greenhouse gas emissions.
  2. Homeowner Information Sheet: how the rating was calculated, a breakdown of your rated energy use, and the details of your building envelope and mechanical equipment as the advisor recorded them. Check these against your house.
  3. Renovation Upgrade Report: recommended upgrades with estimated savings, before-and-after charts of heat loss by building component, your rating before and after the upgrades, the advisor's comments and energy-saving tips.

Expect the reports about two weeks after the visit in Quebec's Rénoclimat program (Québec ↗) and two to three weeks after through Efficiency Manitoba (Efficiency Manitoba ↗).

sections.h2: Who can do an evaluation, and what happens on the day
sections.html:
EnerGuide evaluations are booked through service organizations licensed by NRCan, which send an energy advisor registered with NRCan (NRCan ↗). Advisors must pass NRCan's foundation and energy advisor exams, and every licensed organization must employ a quality assurance specialist. Organizations are independent businesses, not agents of NRCan, and NRCan doesn't endorse any of them; it is not accepting applications from new organizations at present (NRCan ↗). Quebec's 2026 Rénoclimat guide says the EnerGuide Rating System, designed by NRCan, is now administered by Environment and Climate Change Canada (Québec ↗). We could not confirm this change on a federal page, and NRCan's own pages still describe NRCan licensing and registration.

On the day, you sign a consent form (the Notice to Homeowner). The advisor usually starts outside, photographs the exterior, mechanical systems, attic and any wood-burning appliances, and runs a blower door test to measure airtightness; fuel-fired heating and water heating are turned down during the test. The home must be able to hold 22°C, with windows, doors and the building envelope intact. Remove ashes from any wood stove beforehand and have your property tax roll number ready (NRCan ↗). Licensed organizations don't sell door to door or through unsolicited calls or emails.

sections.h2: Pre- and post-retrofit evaluations, and how long a rating stays useful
sections.html:
A pre-retrofit evaluation sets your baseline and gives you the upgrade plan; a post-retrofit evaluation after the work produces a new rating that shows the improvement and, in most rebate programs, unlocks payment. Programs generally require the first evaluation before any work starts, and set their own deadlines: Ontario's Home Renovation Savings needs the follow-up within 180 days of the first visit or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first (program terms ↗), and New Brunswick's Total Home Energy Savings allows 9 months for the work (NB Power ↗).

NRCan's public pages don't give an expiry date for a rating. A rating describes the house on the day it was measured, so renovations or new equipment since then put it out of date, and each program decides which evaluations it accepts. NRCan says the recommendations on an old 0–100 report remain valid, but a current GJ rating needs a new evaluation (NRCan ↗).

sections.h2: What it costs and what programs pay back
sections.html:
NRCan says pre- and post-retrofit evaluations together cost between $600 and $1,000 on average, varying by provider and province, and are typically paid after the service (NRCan ↗). Several programs cut that cost (as of October 2026):

  • Ontario, Home Renovation Savings: $600 back toward both assessments after two or more qualifying upgrades (program ↗).
  • Manitoba, Efficiency Manitoba: a $400 rebate for a pre-retrofit evaluation, if you apply within 90 days.
  • New Brunswick, Total Home Energy Savings: $99 plus HST covers the initial and final evaluations (NB Power ↗).
  • Quebec, Rénoclimat: since October 1, 2026, up to $500 toward an evaluation when you also claim at least one eligible upgrade (Québec ↗); under the earlier rules, $150 plus tax for the first evaluation, refunded except the tax when aid is paid (Québec ↗).

See energy audit costs, or find an advisor near you.

sections.h2: Mistakes to avoid and next steps
sections.html:
• Booking with a company that isn't licensed: check NRCan's list of service organizations by postal code.
  • Starting work before the pre-retrofit evaluation when you want a rebate.
  • Expecting your bills to match the rating, which uses standard conditions.
  • Treating a virtual label as an EnerGuide rating (NRCan ↗).
  • Losing paperwork: keep your file number, reports and paid invoices, which programs with a post-retrofit evaluation ask to see.

Next steps: read what a home energy audit is, check rebates where you live, estimate running costs with the energy cost calculator and build your plan.

faq.q: What is a good EnerGuide rating?
faq.a: Lower is better, and 0 GJ a year means the house produces as much energy as it uses. The most useful comparison is your own reference house on the label, which shows the rating your home would get if built to typical new-home standards.

faq.q: Why doesn't my EnerGuide rating match my energy bills?
faq.a: The rating uses standard thermostat settings, hot water use and occupancy, so it describes the house rather than your household. Weather and habits also change your bills, and extras like a pool or hot tub are listed separately.

faq.q: How much does an EnerGuide evaluation cost?
faq.a: NRCan says $600 to $1,000 on average for the pre- and post-retrofit evaluations together. Programs such as Ontario's Home Renovation Savings ($600 back) and New Brunswick's Total Home Energy Savings ($99 plus HST for both) reduce the cost.

faq.q: Does an EnerGuide rating expire?
faq.a: NRCan's public pages don't give an expiry date. The rating reflects the house on the day it was measured, and each rebate program sets its own rules on which evaluations it accepts.

faq.q: How do I know an energy advisor is legitimate?
faq.a: Book through a service organization on NRCan's list for existing homes, searchable by postal code, or contact NRCan to verify a company. Licensed organizations don't sell door to door or through unsolicited calls or emails.

faq.q: How long does an EnerGuide evaluation take?
faq.a: About two hours for an initial evaluation and about one hour for a follow-up in Ontario's Home Renovation Savings program. Quebec's Rénoclimat lists 2 to 3 hours and 45 to 90 minutes.

title: Reusing your old EnerGuide report
h1: Already had an energy audit? What your old EnerGuide report is still good for
description: Can an older EnerGuide evaluation be reused for rebates, by a new owner or for a cheaper follow-up? What NRCan and 2026 programs say, and what to do next.
blurb: What an older EnerGuide report is still good for, and when programs want a new one.
lede: An evaluation from a few years ago still holds useful information about your house, but most rebate programs want their own evaluation before any work starts. Here is what NRCan and each program say, where the rules are silent, and what to do if the first one was poorly done.

sections.h2: What an old report is still good for
sections.html:
More than 409,000 households completed upgrades through the Canada Greener Homes Grant (NRCan ↗), which took applications from May 2021 to February 2024 and required a pre- and a post-retrofit EnerGuide evaluation (grant steps ↗). Many homeowners therefore already have a report. It is still useful for:

  • Planning. The Renovation Upgrade Report ranks upgrades by estimated savings. NRCan says even the recommendations on old 0–100 labels are still valid (NRCan ↗).
  • Your home's details. The Homeowner Information Sheet records the building envelope and equipment as the advisor found them, and the evaluation included an airtightness (blower door) test.
  • A before picture. If you've upgraded since, the old rating shows where you started.
  • Talking to contractors. Quebec's Rénoclimat notes its report can serve as a reminder for months when you discuss work with a contractor (Québec ↗).

sections.h2: Can it be reused for a rebate? What programs say
sections.html:
There is no national rule on reusing an evaluation; each program sets its own. Here is what current programs say (as of October 8, 2026):

ProgramWill an earlier evaluation count?Key rule
Ontario, Home Renovation SavingsNo. The pre-assessment must be on or after January 28, 2025, before any work, with one of the program's approved organizationsFollow-up within 180 days or by December 31, 2026 (booked by November 30), with the same organization
Quebec, Rénoclimat (rules before October 1, 2026)Yes, for later work: a subsequent evaluation uses your last evaluation as the baseline, with no new pre-work visit$150 plus tax; aid depends on the rating improving between the two most recent evaluations
Quebec, Rénoclimat (since October 1, 2026)Evaluations are optional; up to $500 toward one when you claim an eligible upgradeThe 2026 guide doesn't say whether an evaluation done before October 1, 2026 qualifies; ask the program
Manitoba, Efficiency ManitobaThe $400 pre-retrofit evaluation rebate is paid once per addressApply within 90 days of the evaluation
New Brunswick, Total Home Energy SavingsNot stated; the program starts with its own initial evaluation$99 plus HST for both visits; 9 months to do the work
Canada Greener Homes GrantClosedKeep documents and receipts until March 31, 2028

Ontario's program also asks that the same service organization do both assessments and strongly recommends the same advisor. Joining it again later means a new pre- and post-assessment, and its $600 assessment rebate is paid only once (program requirements ↗). Rénoclimat's old-rules post-work evaluations must be done by March 31, 2027 (Québec ↗). Rénoclimat's subsequent-evaluation page is still online. We read it as describing the rules before October 1, 2026, because it ties aid to a better rating, which the 2026 guide no longer does, so confirm with the program before you rely on it.

sections.h2: Bought a home that already had an evaluation?
sections.html:
NRCan says the homeowner who paid for an evaluation owns the EnerGuide reports, and privacy law lets NRCan share them only with that party. It encourages sellers to share reports with buyers, so ask the seller or your agent for the label, information sheet and upgrade report (NRCan ↗).

The programs we checked treat you as a new participant. Rénoclimat's eligibility page tells new owners they must register themselves and get a new pre-work evaluation (Québec ↗), and its 2026 guide says a buyer can't receive aid for work the previous owner did. Ontario's program requires you to own the home and complete the pre-assessment before work starts. See buying a home.

sections.h2: Getting a copy of your own report
sections.html:
• Start with the service organization that did the evaluation; NRCan lists organizations' phone numbers by postal code (NRCan ↗). Older 0–100 labels show the evaluation date, file number, advisor and organization.
  • If it was for the Canada Greener Homes Grant, your organization also uploaded the reports to the program's online portal, and NRCan advises keeping program documents until March 31, 2028 (NRCan ↗).
  • In Quebec, have your Rénoclimat file number ready and call Rénoclimat customer service at 1 866 266-0008 (Québec ↗).
  • NRCan itself can share reports only with the party that purchased them.

sections.h2: When a fresh evaluation is worth it
sections.html:
• A rebate program requires its own evaluation before work starts, as most of the programs we checked do.
  • You've renovated, air sealed or replaced heating, cooling or water heating equipment since the last visit, so the old rating no longer describes the house.
  • Your label uses the old 0–100 scale (evaluations before 2019): a GJ rating needs a new evaluation.
  • You bought the home and can't get the previous owner's reports.
  • You're planning a heat pump and want current numbers; pair it with a heat loss calculation.

Lower-cost follow-ups exist (as of October 2026): Rénoclimat's subsequent evaluation costs $150 plus tax under the earlier rules, as we read them (Québec ↗), New Brunswick charges $99 plus HST for both visits, and Efficiency Manitoba rebates $400 of a pre-retrofit evaluation once per address (Efficiency Manitoba ↗). Elsewhere, NRCan's average is $600 to $1,000 for a pre- and post-retrofit pair.

sections.h2: If the first evaluation seemed poorly done
sections.html:
Some things are normal. The rating won't match your bills, because it uses standard conditions and applies to the house only (NRCan ↗), and a single small upgrade, such as replacing one window or installing a heat recovery ventilator, may not move the rating (Rénoclimat). Warning signs include details on the information sheet that don't match your home, a missing blower door test, or reports that never arrived.

  1. Write to the service organization with specifics. Licensed organizations must follow NRCan's administrative procedures and employ a quality assurance specialist, who can't review their own files (NRCan ↗). Ask whether your file has been reviewed and can be corrected.
  2. Check that the company is on NRCan's list of service organizations, or contact NRCan to verify it.
  3. If the evaluation was for a program, tell the program: Ontario's Home Renovation Savings (info@homerenovationsavings.ca) or Rénoclimat's administrator (renoclimat@environnement.gouv.qc.ca). Ontario's terms say the program isn't responsible for organizations' acts or omissions (program terms ↗).
  4. Know the limits: NRCan says organizations are independent businesses and it accepts no liability for workmanship (NRCan ↗). We found no published NRCan complaint process for homeowners.
  5. For your next evaluation, choose another licensed organization, unless a program asks you to stay with the first one, as Ontario's does for the follow-up.

sections.h2: Mistakes to avoid and next steps
sections.html:
• Starting work before a required pre-evaluation: Ontario, New Brunswick and Rénoclimat's earlier rules exclude work done before it.
  • Assuming a Greener Homes evaluation counts for Ontario's program: the pre-assessment must be on or after January 28, 2025.
  • Switching organizations partway through a program that asks you to keep the same one.
  • Letting an unsolicited caller “re-inspect” your home: NRCan never authorizes unsolicited inspections. Report scams to energystar@canada.ca and local police (NRCan ↗).

Next steps: find a licensed advisor, check evaluation costs and current programs, estimate savings with the energy cost calculator, and update your plan.

faq.q: Can I use my old energy audit to get rebates?
faq.a: Usually not as your starting point. Ontario's Home Renovation Savings needs a pre-assessment dated January 28, 2025 or later and done before any work, while Quebec's Rénoclimat, under its rules before October 1, 2026, let earlier participants use their last evaluation as the baseline for a subsequent evaluation.

faq.q: Can I get the previous owner's EnerGuide report?
faq.a: Only from the seller. NRCan says the reports belong to whoever paid for the evaluation, and it can share them only with that party.

faq.q: Does an EnerGuide evaluation expire?
faq.a: NRCan's public pages don't give an expiry date. Each program decides which evaluations it accepts, and a rating no longer reflects the house once you've renovated or replaced equipment.

faq.q: Do I have to use the same company for my follow-up evaluation?
faq.a: In Ontario's Home Renovation Savings, yes: the program asks that the same service organization do both, and strongly recommends the same advisor. Other programs set their own rules, so check before switching.

faq.q: My first evaluation seemed rushed. What can I do?
faq.a: Put your concerns in writing to the service organization, which must employ a quality assurance specialist, and tell the program if the evaluation was for one. NRCan treats organizations as independent businesses, and we found no published NRCan complaint process.

faq.q: Is my old 0–100 EnerGuide rating still valid?
faq.a: NRCan says its recommendations are still valid, but the number can't be converted to the current GJ scale. You need a new evaluation for a current rating.
